The TIME SPENT is not really the issue, not if you are being attended to, but when you are not, when you obviously have heart disease symptoms and concerned for clots, it is a long time to just sit and wait and not being care for. Should our conditions not be a priority? After I was admitted to the emerg ward, the nurses were very kind to me and took very good care of me. When I had to go to the restroom it was nasty. I told the nurses and they said they would write it up. I understand that at the time the emergency floor was full of patients on beds even in the hallways because of the flu outbreak. All the more to have the bathrooms scheduled to be cleaned more often in emerg. That is minor issue but an easy one to fix. While on the cardiac floor, the medical staff were amazing. Comment: From attachment - To Whom it May Concern: In reference to my recent hospital experience, I arrived at the hospital emergency department around 8:00 PM on XXXXXXXX with excruciating pain. I explained to the traige nurse that I had an episode with similar pain two years prior and it was diagnosed as Appendicitis. The surgeon at the time treated it with antibiotics, without surgery. She told me to take a seat in the waiting room, but I paced the floor as I couldn't sit much because of the pain. After hours of waiting, I complained to the Traige nurse that the pain was intense and I needed to see a doctor soon. Her response was "other people are in pain as well, you'll have to wait your turn". During my long wait, I complained again, and was told patients were being seen according to priority. Meanwhile, I saw many patients being called in with colds, most of which were children, and many came in after me. I was very upset, and pointed out repeatedly that there was a possibility that I had Appendicitis, but to no avail. After five and half hours, I was finally called in to see doctor. The doctor proceeded to run the necessary tests and ordered a CT scan. I needed to lay down because of the intense pain, but again I was given a chair and I continued to pace the floors. I was told there was no available beds, but I saw two empty beds near the nurse's station, that were empty for some time. Finally around 4:00 AM I was diagnosed with Appendicitis and was given one of those same beds. I spoke to the surgeon on call at 8:00 AM who told me that he would do his best to squeeze me into his schedule of surgeries. I was taken to a room when it became available around 1:00 PM But when the nurses asked me to transfer over onto the other bed, I suddenly felt a more intense pain in my abdomen even worse that the one I was already feeling. I could barely speak from the pain, but I managed to tell them that something had changed. The pain was worse and that I thought something was wrong. No one seemed too concerned. I laid there all afternoon until I was taken to surgery at 5:30 PM where they found that my appendix had ruptured and they found a "mess" inside me. The surgeon was very skilled and still managed to do it laparoscopically. Thankfully, I recovered without infection or other complications, but it was quite an ordeal and I had to deal with the consequences of having had a ruptured appendix. I am extremely sensitive to prescription medications, so in order to somewhat tolerate the antibiotics, I was unable to take the pain medications as needed, resulting in poor pain control. The surgical floor nurses, and aids were extremely helpful, courteous and very hard working. I have nothing but praise for them and for the doctors who cared for me. But I feel that having had to wait for almost twenty four hours with Appendicitis, in excruciating pain, resulted in the perforation. My life was put in danger by a total disregard of the severity of my condition. I believe this was possibly avoidable, and totally unacceptable. I truly hope no-one else is made to experience as I went through. But with our health care system as it is today, I highly doubt it. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX

I was in what I considered to be good health until this incident. I awoke in the morning feeling well, then was suddenly overtaken with dizziness, feeling very weak and nauseous. I was taken to hospital by ambulance and was placed in a cubicle in the emergency department. The nurse I had seemed to be very demanding of me and had a cold bedside manner. I was unable to provide a urine sample and the nurse made several unsuccessful attempts to insert a catheter which was very painful. The doctor informed my family that I was severely dehydrated,had a urine infection, was constipated and had an infection which showed up in my blood tests. A bed pan was placed under me as I laid in bed and I was left like that that most of the day which was very uncomfortable. I was taken by a male attendant who was very pleasant for an ultra sound and was later returned to the emergency department. I found it to be very cold in the emergency cubicle. I was told I was going to be admitted and after spending the whole day in the cubicle, I was taken to a room in the emergency department. The next day I was placed into a room on the sixth floor. The doctors only came to my room on an average of once a day. There was about four different doctors who spoke to me. Only one out of the four doctors seemed to listen to me and tried to explain things to me. He was very gentle and appeared to be sympathetic to what I was going through. The others just came in, talked to me, then left without telling me what was wrong or what to expect. After having placed in my room, I had severe Diarrhea and was placed in isolation. I had several accidents resulting in my bedding and clothing to be messed. The nurses took a long time to respond to my call and I was unable to make it to the bathroom making messes that were very embarrassing and degrading. I found my room to be constantly cold and had to keep asking for more blankets. During the two weeks that I was hospitalized, the only persons to help wash me were family members. My bedding was changed twice, once by my daughter and once by my son, other than that I had to lay in the same bedding. My son after noticing fecal drops on the floor in the bathroom hadn't been cleaned after two days, washed the floor. My family brought in extra blankets to try to keep me warm. I was not at all impressed with the way in which the cleaning staff came into the room, swiped a cloth across my table, along my bed rails and then left. During my stay, I had diarrhea so badly, that I started passing blood. I informed the nurse, who had a doctor come in to examine me. This doctor was very kind and listened to my concerns and was gentle while examining me. He then explained why I was passing blood and appeared to care about my concern. He was the first doctor to explain to me that I had a severe infection which required anti-antibiotics which was the cause of my diarrhea. This was when I first learned that I had also suffered from acute kidney failure. All but one of the nurses who took care of me while I was on the 6th floor were kind and tried their best to care for me, but because there weren't enough of them, appeared to have difficulty keeping up with the demands required for all the patients in their care. The one nurse that came into my room was very uncaring and insisted I had to many blankets and began removing them from my bed. I had to tell her to leave the blankets as I was cold. She walked out of my room and I never saw her again. When I was discharged, I was given papers to sign explaining to watch for C- defissile. I was given prescriptions that the doctor explained to my son how I was to take them. After signing the papers, I had to walk to the exit and out to my ride home. My son had asked a nurse for a wheel chair and was told that none were available. He then went to look for a wheel chair but was unable to locate one. I felt so degraded and embarrassed during this hospital stay.y room was not properly cleaned with dirt and dust in the corners and window sills, along with my son having to wash the bathroom floor because it had not been cleaned. This hospital stay was so awful that I have told my children that should I collapse, leave me in my home and in my own bed to die. It is my personal belief that management in charge of the hospital is over paid and that money for their wages should be used to pay for more nurses and better cleaning staff.

If I was not by his side throughout his entire ordeal, I have no idea what 'care' he would have received in emergency. I hope that these comments will genuinely be reviewed and additional training, support and resources will be offered to staff in the emergency department. Even a sincere smile and a quick genuine check in asking how you are would go a long way! Human dignity is what the health profession should be all about ... should it not? I hope that my father will never need emergency care again, because the thought of that worries me. Again, hope these concerns will be reviewed, and actions can be taken to ensure quality for all! Comment: 2 separate explanations, both very important  Canadian Patient Experiences Survey - Inpatient Care  XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  Hospital stay dates ~ XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX to XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  Additional explanations for questions:  Question #5 ~ During this hospital stay, how often did the doctor's treat you with courtesy and respect?  For the most part, the doctors that I was under the care of were great.  They understood what I had gone through prior to being admitted to the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX on XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and what I was still going through during my hospital stay.  With the exception of 1 doctor ~ On the weekend of XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, my current doctor was off and a replacement doctor was on call.  (Don't remember his name)  I had been suffering from C-Diff for a few months and a few selected nurses were getting unsympathetic of my constant spoiling of my undergarments and frustrated on having to continually change them and me, so upon a request by a nurse (not sure which one), this doctor ordered a "butt plug" to be put into action so that the nurses no longer needed to clean me because everything would go through a tube into a bag and therefore less attention to my c-diff needs (cleaning and changing me) was necessary.  I would like to note that the doctor never came to me and explained what the procedure for this butt plug was and why he felt it necessary for this course of action ... had he spoke to my doctor that was my ongoing care doctor?  No ... I was extreme pain, 24/7 ... no drugs could take away the pain ... I begged to have it taken out ... and the nurses said no.  My husband asked for someone to check it to see if maybe it was put in wrong causing the extreme pain and they re-inserted it upon my husband's request but it was still unbearable pain.  I couldn't sleep, eat and was crying constantly because of the pain.  One night sometime around XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX ... My husband couldn't bare to hear my screams and crying and requested for a nurse to take another look at the plug ... to see why it was hurting her so much?  There was a nurse (I think her name was XXXXXX) that explained that she would come and take a look at it and talk to me and my husband.  This nurse was not on regular call on this floor, (a more mature nurse)  She was visiting the floor to see how things were going ... she did this regularly on each floor of the hospital to make sure things were running smoothly ... she had been a nurse for XXXX XXXXXX years ... so she knew her stuff.  When the nurse went to check the butt plug, she asked why was this butt plug put in, in the first place?  She seemed very upset ... my husband explained it was the call of the nurses and the on call doctor because of my c-diff and the constant changing.  The nurse explained that she was pulling it out immediately because my c-diff was not a liquid that could easily pass through the tube, it was having some solids and the extreme pain was because the "poop" couldn't get through the tube and was backing up in my bowels!  This nurse was very upset and angry that this procedure was done and had put me in this terrible pain.  She called in the nurse on the floor for my room, told her to gather all the nurses to the station.  My husband listened to the discussion at the station with all the nurses and care people, she told them that the nurse on that shift for my care, would check me every half hour and if cleaning was needed it would be done ... no questions.  She also stated taht the cream they were using to subside my pain in the groin area was not the cream to be used and they knew better.  She ordered the cream necessary and told the nurse to cream me every half hour!  This nurse explained to the nurses on the floor that night, that this procedure was unnecessary and that she didn't care if they had to clean me every half hour, that was part of their job as being a nurse ... not everything about being a nurse or care provider was all roses!ithin a few hours, my terrible pain subsided and I was able to sleep without pain.  If it wasn't for my husband seeing the extreme pain and seeing me in tears and being able to bare me in this pain and him going for a 2nd time to have someone check me and the tube, I don't know if I could have made it through this situation.  This one nurse was my saviour and I can't thank her enough.  NOTE*  VERY IMPORTANT ... I would like to mention ... that this same "on call weekend doctor" was the one who was watching me try to get used to using the wheelchair, and he stated/told me that he was pleased to see that I was trying the wheelchair and getting used to it because I was NEVER going to walk again!  How dare he say that to a patient (any patient!) when he has no idea who he is talking to, what they have gone through and what their mental state is or was at that time!  What if that patient didn't have the family support that I had, what if that patient was at a critical state of mind situation?  Would that push that patient over the edge of fighting and possibly give up on their fight to survive?  Maybe he should think twice about his words next time!  It could mean the difference between going home or not going home but to another unthinkable place ... thank God for my family and their strength and perseverance in making sure I know I am strong and will make it through!  Question #14 ... During you hospital stay, how often did the hospital staff do everything they could to help you with your pain?  For the most part, the answer is sometimes ... but there were also times when I was in pain (see above!) and the nurses and care providers were unsympathetic to my needs ... I was not one to constantly ask for pain meds but when I needed it (couldn't bare the pain) I asked for some help with the pain and sometimes the pain meds were not provided.  Question #16 ~ Before giving you any new medicine, how often did the hospital staff tell you what the medicine was for?  There were several occasions where new meds or an increase of meds levels was given, we (myself, my husband or my daughter) where not explained what was now being given to me, if new or increased and why?  For example ... I was on a seizure medication and at the smallest level/amount due to my body's acceptance level ... At least the amount I was able to communicate and be active in my health care but when it was increased (unknown to my doctor at the time of my care) another doctor "on call" increased my seizure meds which once again put me back into my coma like state.  When I was in this state, I could not effectively communicate to my family of doctors what was going on ... when my husband found out this was done, he connected with my doctor who was in charge of my care and he was confused why my seizure meds were increased ... He immediately went to the "on call doctor" and the nurses and changed the meds back to my level my body could handle and I slowly came out of my coma like states ... (took about 2 days) ... he stated that would not happen again.  On several occasions, my husband and/or daughter would have to continuously asked the nurses dispersing my meds, what meds I was getting (at all my meals) to make sure they were the appropriate levels and necessary meds.  On one occasion my daughter had to decline the meds being given to me on a lunch hour because it was taken off of my list of meds by my doctor but was still being dispersed to me ... because I wasn't in my own state of mind or unable to know what I was receiving, I thank God for my family for being on top of things and knowing what the new meds or new levels were for my continuous treatment of care.  Question #19 ~ During this hospital stay, did doctors, nurses or other hospital staff talk with you about whether you would have the help needed when you left the hospital?  You're kidding, right?  NO!!!  On the week date of XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX ... a meeting with the discharge staff was scheduled with myf and my family.  We (the family) requested that not only the discharging staff be in attendance but as well the 2 doctors who were my main care doctors (Dr. X and Dr. XXXXXX) to be in attendance at this meeting.  We were told by the discharging staff, the doctors were not necessary for this discharge meeting.  This was unnerving to my family ... we had only met the one person in this discharging staff and the other 2 staff members, we had never met and I am not sure if they had any idea of what my status had been over the past 7 years.  My husband and daughter were in the meeting because they had been by my side for the past 7 months (every day, almost every hour of my terrible medical history in the 2 hospitals) and so they knew what was at stake.  The discharging staff didn't even given my family the chance to explained why they did not agree and were concerned for my release and the possible complications of my release so early.  The decision had been made and they or myself had no say in this discharge.  The discharging staff told myself and my family that there would be assistance through the PSW program (XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX) for us to use to assist me in my "release to home care" transition.  My husband was concerned that I still had an appointment for my 2nd fecal transplant scheduled for the day of my release and if they were to release me in the morning of my scheduled appointment in XXXXXXXX for this fecal transplant ... That we would not have any transportation to and back from this appointment and taht this put us in a rough situation knowing I couldn't travel in a car and the expense of a transportation vehicle would cost my family just short of $400.00 for the day!  My husband and daughter begged the staff to at lease let me be discharged in the afternoon so that the hospital could assist us in this important appointment and transportation.  The discharging staff said they couldn't guarantee this and left us waiting until the day of release no knowing if we would be able to make the appointment.  FInally, the hospital agreed to have the patient care transportation company take me to my appointment and then to be returned to my home ... for my release of the hospital.  NOTE*  When we were at this appointment in XXXXXXXX for my 2nd fecal transplant ... we were told that I would need to be under strict doctor's care so taht they could look out for any adverse reactions to the transplant.  When we (my family) told the doctor there that I was not going back to the hospital and instead had been discharged about an hour ago ... he was very upset and perplexed ... because it was now the family's responsibility to take care of me and look for any and all adverse reactions and give strict medical care. I arrived at the Emergency Department with a highly swollen seroma containing a blood clot, a side effect of a double XXXX carried out in XXXXXXXX. The surgeon who carried out the XXXX (he operates out of XXXXXXXX), on seeing some photos, urged me to immediately go to an Emergency Department, as the site was very, very swollen. He said to request the site to be given an ultrasound and drained, as the swelling was starting to bruise the newly healed incisions. He also said to print out his e-mail recommendations, which included his personal phone number, saying he would be happy to speak to any doctor or surgeon who was seeing me and saying that as my surgeon, he was ordering the drainage. I was in pain when I entered the hospital, the swelling was so big I couldn't move without the stretched skin hurting. My XXXX were starting to stretch and warp as a result as well.   Although there were only four people in the Emergency Department, nurses weren't available to speak to, and the wait was very long. After being admitted, I, and the other patients, were brought into another waiting room -- I say without exaggeration that I was waiting for hours and hours to be seen by a doctor. Again, there were four patients -- the other three also expressed concern; one had arrived with a severely swollen toe that had gone purple. After the check-in, nobody checked on us, spoke to us, looked at us.   After the hours of waiting, an Emergency Department doctor looked at the seroma, told me, 'that's a seroma', assured me that 'it's a very common XXXX after a XXXX and that 'it's very easily drained.' After prodding and poking it some more (ignoring my saying that I was in pain and terrified by the swelling), he said 'I don't feel comfortable carrying out this procedure, I'll call in a surgeon, it won't be a long wait.' I was a bit frustrated -- if, in his words, seromas are common and very easily drained, why can't a practicing attending doctor in a hospital do it? But I decided I could be patient. I didn't want to be XXXX or demanding. I agreed that I would wait for a surgeon. The doctor disappeared for about a full hour -- I had no idea what was happening, if he had been distracted by someone else, if he was still getting the surgeon ... I felt very helpless and unsure.   After the hour had passed, he returned, saying, 'good news! I found a surgeon who will come to see you, it won't be long -- maybe a couple of hours.' He said this with a straight face. 'It won't be long -- maybe a couple of hours.' I have no idea what patience he expects from people. If he'd just phrased it differently, like, say, 'I did find a surgeon, it will take a while for him to see you - it could take a couple of hours, is that ok?', and checked on my pain levels, I wouldn't have been frustrated. But he acted like I had won the lottery or something. I was speechless, but I didn't want to leave without having the seroma drained. (I'm still tremendously disappointed that if a seroma is as easily drained as EVERY doctor, surgeon or otherwise, tells me it is, that this doctor felt he wasn't up to it.)   So I waited again. He wasn't lying when he said it would take a couple of hours. It took over two hours, sitting in the waiting room, nobody speaking to me, nobody checking up on me, me being in pain sitting there, until the surgeon arrived. I understand that Emergency Departments can get busy, but it wasn't busy that day. I was there. I could see that it wasn't. Close to five hours of waiting in the Emergency Department and the only people to speak to me had been the nurses checking me in and the doctor who didn't treat me and left. I felt very helpless and ignored. The surgeon arrived -- not wearing a name tag, so I don't know who it was. He didn't introduce himself. He had a brief look at the XXXXX, said 'the bruising isn't that bad' and that I should go home. He didn't 'feel draining to be necessary'. I told him the drainage had n ordered by my XXXXXXXX surgeon, I showed him the e-mail, and the phone number, begging him, BEGGING him to please just call the XXXXXXXX surgeon to speak to him about it. I asked to please just get an ultrasound, as requested by my XXXXXXXX surgeon, because the size of the seroma was worrying. He refused that, too. He said I was worrying too much and that the fluid would just get re-absorbed into my body. He told me to go home. I asked him what I should do if it doesn't get better, as over the course of a week, it had just ballooned and gotten worse and worse with no sign of stopping. He said 'if it turns yellow or looks infected, come back in, but until then, stay home, take some painkillers, and wait.' In so many words. He refused me treatment entirely.  I do find it VERY suspicious that the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX surgeon refused to treat me, a XXXXX individual, currently XXXXXX. Would he have treated a ciswoman with a XXXXXXXXXX seroma the same way? Did my XXXXX identity inform his decision to ignore my XXXXXXXX surgeon's requests, to refuse to do so much as take an ultrasound, to refuse my pleas for treatment, to ignore the fact that I was in pain? Obviously, I can't prove that. But it's certainly how it felt at the time. And XXXX individuals being denied medical treatment isn't exactly new.   This is not an XXXXX, this is simply how it felt.  XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX is home to surgeons, doctors, and nurses, who have helped my XXXXX and actively operated on me and have been nothing but kind to me. I'm not speaking about everyone working at the hospital. But this ONE XXXX, whose name I still don't know, because again, no name tag or introduction -- he DID make me feel like he was denying treatment based on my being a XXXX.   Leaving the Emergency Department I was in pain, felt like nobody cared what was happening to my health, felt like nobody cared that I had been in the department for six hours and not received any treatment or advice on what to do next whatsoever.   Panicked, I made an emergency appointment with my general practitioner, who was immediately alarmed by the size of the seroma, referred me to an ultrasound clinic -- the ultrasound was done the next day -- and was rushed to another surgeon's practice to begin draining immediately. I will not name names here. There's little point to it. The surgeon I'm seeing to have the seroma drained has been working on draining it for the past 8 weeks. It's a slow process, as the fluid pocket had swollen to such extremes that the first draining yielded nearly XXXX of fluid all in all, and had to be carried out over the course of two days as there was too much and too widely spread to drain in a day. As a solid comparison, the seroma contained enough fluid to fill a Coca Cola can. The chest had gone from flat to about a B-cup as part of the swelling.   And yet the surgeon who saw me at the Emergency Department said draining it wasn't necessary and to just go home.   Not just that. The seroma had formed around a blood clot and the fluid was a blackish red, had a thick viscosity in places. The surgeon who is draining it -- is still draining it, I went to see him again today for my latest appointment. He has explicitly said that there was absolutely no medical scenario in which this fluid would have been reabsorbed into the body, it would've only brought about further health complications, and that I did the right thing in going to my family doctor and him for a second opinion. He has openly told me that draining a seroma of this size was the only possible answer to the situation, and that he vehemently disagreed with the surgeon I saw at the Emergency Department. (He did say that yes, surgeons are allowed to refuse procedures, and not knowing who the surgeon in question was, he couldn't speak as to why the decision was made.)   I've now spent two months in a compression vest and getting the seroma drained ag and again -- but at least it's being done by someone who takes incredibly good care to drain it carefully and painlessly, who never refused any kind of treatment, who sees me in a timely manner, who makes follow-up appointments to see how things are progressing. He could also speak to other post-surgery effects I was experiencing and is doing so with compassion, patience, and respect. He never dismisses me nor my concerns.   I try not to think about what would've happened to my surgical site if I had listened to the surgeon at the General Hospital who told me to 'just go home and wait'. I'm glad I found proper care elsewhere. I think it's profoundly disappointing to have to hunt for it, again, even after my XXXXXXXX surgeon -- whose medical orders and opinion were completely ignored by the surgeon at the hospital -- wrote an entire e-mail specifying what he required to be done, and where to reach him immediately.  This is not my first time having a bad experience at the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX Emergency Department. A while ago, I had a XXXX performed, and at some point during the healing process, the incision site started to seep blood profusely. I was in the waiting room waiting to be seen for hours -- I wasn't given dressing, I wasn't given attention, I was bleeding from a fresh surgical site and I was simply told to get some toilet paper from the washrooms and hold it against the wound while I waited. For hours. I wasn't demanding to skip to the front of the line, I was just hoping to maybe be seen by a nurse who could apply a temporary, sterile dressing so that I might avoid infection and not sit in the waiting room with toilet paper clutched to my abdomen, afraid of what might have happened.   This has been my last visit to the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX Emergency Department. I may in the future still be referred to surgeons in XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, and I will certainly still go - a lot of good surgeons I've met work there. I am not tarring them all with the same brush. The vast majority of XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX is incredibly competent, caring, and kind. But these two experiences, the last experience in XXXXX, at the Emergency Department, has made it very obvious to me that I will not receive respectful treatment there -- or indeed any treatment there, as was the case. Looking at online reviews of the hospital, I am not the only one with such experiences. I don't know what the issue with the Emergency Department is, but someone really needs to sort it out.

Upon arrival to the XXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXX I was taken seriously very quickly and rushed into a room in the XXXXXX. However, after entering my room the care went downhill fast. The nurse on duty was kind and helpful but the care was not. I was admitted for appendicitis and was in a severe amount of pain. I had my partner XXX with me and we had to stay in what the nurse said used to just be a room with a chair all night on our first night. This was the night I was in my worst pains, and the bed was a simple trolley bed with hardly any padding and my partner slept on a plastic chair all night which did not even really fit in the 'room'. We were both confused after I was admitted why I still had to stay in XXXXXX for the night. At which this moment I immediately wished we had chosen a different hospital, but due to the amount of pain I was in, we had no choice but to stay. My next complaint was what happened to us after the removal of my appendix, which happened the next evening. I was put into a room with two beds with my partner after my surgery. Around 2 am we were abruptly woken up stating we had relocated to a ward because someone in XXXXXX needed a bed. You can imagine how upsetting this is; when I myself had to stay over night in XXXXXX with appendicitis pains and here I am the very next night being relocated to a different room with more people to accommodate someone from XXXXXX, it just did not sit right with us. Also, to be relocated at that hour right after my surgery was not easy for me mentally and physically. That night, I also experienced one of the only nurses who I found rude and uncaring. When expressing my pains she had no sympathy and out right said that to me. She was getting 'annoyed' with how many times I had to call her to use the bathroom, and made comments about how I have no right to complain about pain because I have never birthed a child. On a side note, other than that one nurse, the nurses were very caring and sympathetic to my pains. Also, after my stay, I took longer than usual to heal. I was not told of the symptoms I would have after wards nor how to eat or take care of myself. So when I had trapped gas I was in a lot of pain and did not realize it was tied to the operation. Wish I could have had better follow up in that regard. Also, I went to the doctor about three weeks after because I was still not eating or getting any better, only to find out I had picked up an infection from XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX ... I will say I was grossed out on multiple occasions on how dirty this hospital was. The bathrooms were always dirty and smelly. The shower I had to use while staying there was ancient and not maintained; I had very little privacy. There was also an outbreak in my room with an infection and we were all kicked out to have it cleaned. I did not have the strength to carry all of my belongings out. The cleaners came in to disinfect our room so we were all safe from the virus and myself and another patient watched them throw our belongings out of the room onto the hard floor without any care. Everyone who was sharing that room, including family members were very disappointed to see how little care was given to our personal belongings. Luckily, nothing was broken.  The last thing I have to say, is that months later, I received a bill from XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX about my stay. This was for my stay in a 'semi-private' room. Which I did not request and it did not happen as I previously mentioned we were kicked out only after hours of being put into a two person room. I called the financial woman (whom I don't have her name in front of me), I do believe she was listed on the letter as supervisor, and left her multiple voice mails to clear this up. To this day I have never received a reply and have no idea where I stand on that issue either. In conclusion, the XXXXXXXXX room was one of my biggest complaints, along with being relocated immediately after my surgery. I would not recommend this hospital to anyone and ar speaking to more locals they shared the same views. It is clear something needs to change and I hope you take my comments seriously, because our health is important!

Comment: (1) There should be private rooms for after delivery (2) The wheelchairs that take you to post delivery are too small (not for every size person)

1 - During my stay, my husband wanted to stay overnight with me and the baby, but the rooms are not set up to allow for this as the chair are just rockers (uncomfortable). I know other hospitals are more accommodating. 2 - Food used to be much better, when we were here in XXXX
Code: Access/Coord of Care, Dietary/Service, Families/Friends, Physical Comfort

Comment: 1 Food was good but portions were small 2 Personal property was left behind and was lost!!

1 small thing: roommate was having blood flow/clot blockage problems through a catheter - severe excruciating pain, and blood reservoir emptying in our bathroom. At one point there was a little blood left on bathroom floor - appeared to be splash from a nurse emptying the reservoir into toilet. I cleaned it up - not a big problem, but maybe something they should've noticed, could've been more careful. 2. My bed had some new air pillow mechanism that extended underneath my body and would on its own periodically inflate/deflate different parts of it - I believe in an effort to move my body weight to increase comfort / avoid bed pressure point soreness - great - BUT - eventually I wanted to stop it so I could just sleep as it did tend to stop me from getting to sleep! I tried to turn it off but couldn't fully figure out how, later I mentioned it to a nurse who didn't seem to be able to figure it out either. Again not a major problem but might of helped in sleeping. I imagine they are new and maybe not fully understood how to operate by everyone? BUT - not complaining - overall stay was 500% better than 1st operation stay in XXXXXXXX.
Code: Access/Coord of Care, Housekeeping/Room, Nurse/Nurse aide, Physical Comfort

Comment: 1 The nurses who took blood test poked the left arm few times then switched to the rt arm. Left wrist 3 bad bruises last 2 weeks. 2 Nurses kept no in bed without a bell. I was tethered I.V. to a computer. Closed the doors for about an hour. I had to call 911 for help!!
Code: Access/Coord of Care, Continuity/Transition, Nurse/Nurse aide, Physical Comfort

Comment: 1 The private room I was in was very hot we asked the nurses to contact someone to have a look. Problem was not fixed during the 2 days I was in hospital. My friend gave birth 3 weeks after me and she had the same complaint 2 I gave birth on XXXXXXXX so there was no lactation consultant until XXXXXX, a few hours before being released from the hospital. My baby didn't latch on due to my flat nipples I had to give formula to my baby. 1. The most shocking aspect of my ED visit was that the doctors FORGOT ABOUT ME at the end, so I ended up being in the ED for over 10 hours. Initially, I was impressed that I was given an ECG within 10 minutes of my arrival as my family doctor asked me to go immediately to the ED due to chest tightness, to rule out heart attack or pulmonary embolism (have a history of PE). I then had blood tests. Then I had both the ECG and blood tests repeated but the nurses did not explain why. I was told I would need to have a CT scan but then nothing happened. I arrived at 1 pm. At around 6 pm I asked a nurse if I could go to get something to eat but she advised I sit and wait in case the doctor comes. I had not eaten since the previous night. I had not drunk anything since I arrived as I had my mask on due to Covid and could not go out of the waiting area for the above reason. Eventually I asked another nurse if I had been forgotten because all the other people who arrived at about the same time had been discharged or were undergoing further investigation. After a while I asked the same nurse (who had nothing to do with my case at all), if I had been forgotten because I was still waiting. I then overheard this nurse making a phone call to someone, saying the patient had been forgotten and had been there since the previous shift. By now it must have been almost 10 pm. How can one of the best hospitals in Canada 'forget' a patient? Surely there must be systems and processes in place, showing how long a patient has been in the ED and how long it has been since the last test or conversation. 2. I have had PE before, but when I was living abroad in Asia and thankfully was treated in one of the best hospitals in the country. So when I was told I would have a CT scan during this ED visit, I was ready for that, but it never happened. I had to ask the doctor why and the resident (not an ED doctor), explained that they did 2 sets of tests to compare the results and said it was not needed. I accepted that but think that the first nurse who said I would need a CT scan could have said 'depending on the test results first'. In summary, I was a bit confused and frankly it would have given me more peace of mind to have had the CT scan but I accept that they relied on the D-Dimer test. So for several hours, I was under the impression I was waiting for a CT scan and assumed that is why I had been left waiting for so long only to find out that they decided it was not needed. 3. I wish I had been provided more information at each stage e.g. We will now show the ECT and blood test results to the doctor. Then he/she will decide if more tests are needed. We expect this to take about xyz amount of time before a doctor will see you. If the results are fine, you should be free to go in about x hours. In fact I never met the doctor whose name appeared on the sheet of paper with the results because a resident saw me instead. I was wondering why I never met the doctor who reviewed the results. I concluded they were too busy and had to bring in other doctors and I was not considered high priority. In summary, the information provision was poor. 4. For ambulatory patients in the ED, it would be helpful if we could be told 'I am nurse xyz. If you have questions while you wait, you can look for me and ask me. Or you can go to xyz place or person to ask them. I was just left waiting there like a widget waiting for the next part of the factory assembly line and it was only when I was desperately hungry and tired after being there 10 hours (and not eaten for over 24 hours since my last meal was the night before), that I plucked up the courage to talk to another nurse, because the first one who did my blood test had left. Perhaps the 'patient care' experience could be improved for those who are not critically ill in the ED. There is a lot of waiting and wondering. We are also human beings, not just a number. Furthermore, my father died that same ED just a few months before I had to visit for my own health matter, so I was not too happy about being forgotten and being left there for so long, not knowing why I was still there. When my father died, the care he received was outstanding, perhaps because the medical staff involved showed extra attention given it was an end of life situation, but on this occasion I was disappointed overall. I was 1impressed that I was seen to so quickly when I explained my family doctor insisted I go to the ED right away to check my heart, but then things seemed to fall apart after that initial care. 5. Documentation: I was surprised that I had to request some documentation so I could explain to my family doctor what the outcome was. In the world class hospital I was a patient at, in a country in Asia, patients were automatically given documentation at the end of their visit. Here, I had to ask and the resident said the doctor would be able to access the systems of XXXX but I said they are not connected to XXXX so she had to go and print out the blood test results but could not give me the ECG graphs. I wish the XXXXXXX could give even a 2 line summary of the outcome, to each patient, to give to their doctor (and to have a record of what was done, and what the conclusion was). In my case, the doctor had no suggestion as to what may have been the cause of my chest tightness and said to follow up with my family doctor, so after 10 hours, I had no idea what may have happened. Having said all of this, I am grateful for the care I received. Please accept these comments in the constructive spirit in which they are intended. My family doctor had to practically insist and urge me to go to the ED knowing how reluctant I was due to Covid, so waiting for 10+ hours (I arrived at 1 and left at 10.30 pm), in a potentially high risk Covid location was not a good experience. I think I would have to be practically dying to return there.

First of all I am grateful of the health care system of Canada. Which give me the chance of this surgery (knee replacement). And I am grateful of all the staff of XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. What they have done for me during that period.

First of all, I had issues with food services while staying in the hospital after my surgery. We were in contact with them regarding my several anaphylactic food allergies and I don't feel they handled my requirements as well as they should have, especially in a medical hospital dealing with health issues. My hospital stay once admitted into the hospital for surgery was very organized and I felt well looked after by the nurses. My surgeon was very helpful and made me feel as comfortable as I could be about my procedure. Before being admitted into the hospital, I had a very long stay in the emergency room waiting room and then in the next waiting room and then to see any medical staff with long periods of time in between while being in large amounts of pain that I needed a surgery for that day. I went to the emergency room late at night and once waiting for hours to be seen and admitted. I was told then that there was no ultrasound testing available until the following morning and there was nothing more they could do for me until then in terms of diagnosis. So I was told I could wait until morning in a chair in the waiting room or go home and then come back for an testing appointment in the morning. However, I feel I couldn't make an informed decision as there wasn't any discussion or advisement that I likely needed to continue pain medication to manage my pain levels overnight. I arrived the next morning to my ultrasound appointment and it had not been scheduled as there was an error in the communication somewhere from the emergency department staff to the radiology department and had to wait longer for them to fit me in. Once I completed the tests and had to go through the admitting process once again, I did not see the emergency room to get any pain medication or discuss my condition in a timely fashion, in fact I was seen by the surgeon before I saw the emergency doctor. It was approximately 12-14 hours between getting pain medication at night and then after waiting for re-admission and diagnosis. Had I been informed or recommended that I would potentially need pain medication and not able to receive anything for such a long period of time, I would not have listened to the doctor's advice to be 'happier in my own bed for a few hours'. Since there was nowhere for me to sleep or be comfortable for the few hours before my appointment, I see why they suggested going home and I would have been fine going home to sleep for a few hours if I were allowed to be admitted to the 'yellow area' in the hospital for medication while waiting for my appointment.

We have a very extensive history with our OB, some of that history being of very difficult circumstances where we lost a child at full term and birthed him at XXX. We were with our OB for years, and our pregnancies and births were very high anxiety. One of the doctors that attended us did not seem to have been versed on our history, and therefore caused us very high anxiety during our last experience leading up to the birth of our daughter. Or she was versed but lacked the empathy that would have assured us that we had a plan that made everyone comfortable. Either way, we were quickly reassured by our OB that we were in good hands, and he was keeping tabs on us throughout the process. We are certainly patients that did not benefit from the hospital's new rules of the on call being the only attending physician. We do not feel that this is practical for us nor is it emotionally appealing to know, especially with our history, that we will very likely have a doctor that we do not know attend the birth. Frankly, we feel this should be reviewed and changed. it comes across as the hospital prioritizing money over patient care. This stay, in terms of nursing care, was very supportive in regards to breastfeeding. I received a lot of support from the attending nurses, from birth to baby unit. I had some difficulty breastfeeding due to pain from a wound on both nipples, and was shown a hold that allowed me to continue to feed my daughter more comfortably. Breastfeeding was important to me and I felt that this was very well supported. I also did not feel undue pressure to breastfeed - formula feeding was also made to feel like a comfortable option without judgment. One more note: for the birth of my second son XXXXXXXXXXXX, the nurses that attended us when we went into labor read our history, and one of them was incredibly empathetic and asked us what room our first son had been born in. This strikes me as the epitome of carelessness. I stated firmly that I would not allow my husband back into that room, that if nothing more safe could be arranged, i would take him out of XXX. They indicated that even in emerg or in any other room that had been sanitized, airborne particles might present the same situation. The waiting area itself is somewhat comfortable (the phone charging station is a bonus!) but there is nothing to do while waiting. A few out of date CAA magazines littered the tables and the TV didn't work. People in pain or discomfort need distraction, and they need some indication of progress (even if it's a placebo). I understand there are limits; however, an emergency room visit isn't just part of an ordinary day for patients the way it is for the staff. People are scared, confused, hurt, anxious, uncertain, alone, or even unable to communicate properly. I almost missed being served. I chose to sit in a chair in the back, around a corner. There were several chairs set up back there, with plexiglas panels, clearly intended for patients to wait there. I had been sitting for hours, and was tired, but was luckily listening closely (I could have had earbuds in for God sake). So I just barely heard my name, went running to see if I had been called. The nurse had already gone back in to the room behind the glass, and was looking at the computer, I imagine getting the name of the next patient. I banged and banged on the glass, probably looking crazy, and finally got someone to come out and straighten things out. I was very close to waiting for 3-4 hours and not getting to see a doctor. Very, very bad practice. PLEASE tell the nurses to be THOROUGH in looking for patients EVERYWHERE that has been set up to accommodate people waiting, and to NOT call out from next to their work station. PLEASE! Otherwise great visit, if long. Both doctors I saw were fantastic--attentive, thoughtful, concerned, serious, thorough. Nurses were otherwise mostly great. But this was almost a BIG problem, and had me quite panicked under already difficult circumstances, and for no good reason. Please ask all nurses to walk the extra six metres.

It was obvious, even in the ambulance that this was more of a precautionary action on the part of the paramedics because there was no rush in getting me to the hospital, nor was there any rush on the part of Emergency staff, once we had arrived to attend to me. I was perfectly fine with this because by the time we arrived I knew that I wasn't going to be, nor should I be, a high priority patient. I only had a couple of issues with what happened during my time at the hospital. The first is that, when I was asked to wait in the Emergency Department waiting room I immediately noticed the large TV that regularly listed the anticipated wait times for various colour priorities, however, nobody told me if I was blue or yellow, so I had to go ask one of the admissions staff which colour I was so that I could get a sense of how long I could anticipate waiting. This brings me to my second issue. I work for one of the Emergency Services myself so I'm very well aware that as an Emergency Department the staff have no way of knowing when a patient might come in who needs immediate attention of the staff. What was somewhat dispiriting was that it was around 2200 hrs when I found out I was a yellow and the wait time was estimated to be about 3 hrs. I assumed based upon these projections that I would get out of the hospital at some point between 0100 and 0200 hours. But as the hours ticked by nothing happened. It was around 0300 hours, a full 5 hours after I first saw that the anticipated wait time was going to be around 3 hours before I was brought to a 'exam room' if you will, where I was left alone for the next 1.5 hours. I didn't get released from the hospital until just before 0500 hours and had to go to work at 0700 hours. I question the value of providing anticipated wait times to the public when the Emergency Department is unable to come remotely close to meeting those times. Everyone understands that in a hospital emergency department there may be unanticipated delays but when a 3 hour wait is nearly doubled, the TV becomes a source of resentment rather than a source of useful information. Comment: A 12 hour visit to the ER is simply unacceptable. At some point, someone should have been able to make a judgment call and just told me to go home. Of course, if I were in life threatening danger, that would be ill advised but, everyone knew I wasn't. I understand this is a symptom of a much greater problem and that's the lack of doctors and family doctors. Granted. However, I came to the ER knowing that I was not in immediate danger but without any other options. I figured I would end up in Zone B. Lo and behold, both the triage nurse and the registration nurse assured me that is where I was going. That was until a third nurse showed up and told them 'no more patients to Zone B. The doctor isn't taking anymore over there.' I was then told to go back to the waiting room and wait there because Zone B was closing early that day. Everyone, including myself, knew that I should be a part of a different process but I was told to go there anyway. I then spent the next 8 hours in the waiting room BEFORE being sent to a private room where I waited another 3 - 4 hrs before seeing a doctor. Clearly there were no doctors in the building. Why wasn't I told? Why was I not given the opportunity to make a decision about whether or not staying overnight in the ER waiting room was right for me? I'm sure the answer is liability. Maybe then, a doctor should have to review the triage notes of those who are already in the waiting room before leaving for the day. If they deem it appropriate for someone to come back the next day, that person should be able to make that decision. Don't just leave people in the dark for hours on end. Everyone was in agreement that my problem was non-urgent. Why was the smarter idea to force me to stay at a hospital, overnight, without sleep, instead of just sending me home? This is particularly frustrating because I came to the ER with chronic leg pain that is exacerbated by long periods of sitting. I came to the ER hoping for a solution to a problem that was made quite a bit worse by my visit to the ER itself. It took literal days for my leg pain to subside to the point where it was when I decided to risk a visit to the ER in the first place. I also know that volume of patients wasn't what was preventing me from seeing a doctor. The same patients who were there when I arrived, were the same people who sat and waited with me all night. No one else added themselves to the equation. It was me, 4 or 5 other patients, in the waiting room, for literally half of an entire day. I get it. For the staff of the hospital, this was a no-win situation. You tell me to go home and I die? The hospital is liable. I get it . But that's ridiculous. I'm not sure what the solution is and it's not my job to provide you with one but it is imperative that it is figured it out. The last thing people need is to be sitting in an ER for 12 hrs during a global pandemic. To finish off, I want to mention that after several visits in the last 2 years, the doctor I saw that night (early morning) was finally able to help me start on a path to solving my chronic pain by ordering two different MRI's. I have been begging doctors to take my problem seriously for years and this doctor finally did. For that, I am appreciative. Everything that lead up to that point is inexcusable and I hope this comment is taken as an opportunity to help change these processes. Thanks for the opportunity to submit this comment.
Code: Access/Coord of Care, Admit/Registration, Doctor/Physician, Emergency Dept, Information/Education, Nurse/Nurse aide, Physical Comfort, Radiology

It caused great anxiety as soon as I knew we had to - could not eat and had a panic attack as well - history of anxiety and panic. X-ray following XXX XXXXXXXXXXXX - the way this was carried out it, was the most excruciatingly painful experience of my entire surgery process. There has to be a more humane way of doing this essential x-ray. Either do it immediately after surgery while the patient is still under some anaesthetic or devise another method of moving the patient from the bed to the x-ray platform and vice versa. This was the only thing in my entire stay that brought me to tears! 4. Respect that each person reacts differently to anaesthetic and the length of time to come out of anaesthetic and spinal freezing. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX NRC Health XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX Re: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX Dear Sir or Madam: I have helped my father, XXXXXXXXXXXXX, fill out the enclosed survey. There wasn't a section to let you know of some rather important concerns. Thus, this letter. We feel it is important to make you aware of procedures that seem to be lacking in the care of "blind" people at the XXX, most importantly the assistance required at meal times. xxxxxxxxxxxxx I suggest the following: - On the large white board in the patient's room, please write in that the person is blind. - When approaching the blind person to do any sort of procedure, please let the patient know. They usually have a strong sense of "left" and "right". - If the blind person has their eyes closed, it is not necessarily because they are asleep. Also, as with my father he is hard of hearing. In this case, the caregivers need to speak louder. My father is still as sharp as a tack! - In speaking to a food service worker, she told me that their job was simply to get the meals delivered to many people and that if my father needed extra help, then I should speak to his nurse. Speaking to his nurse the answer was that when my father gets delivery of food tray he should push the call bell and when the nurse arrives she will decide when she, or another, will have time to help him. You and I both know that this could take time! - So, on delivery of food tray by food service I am requesting that the blind patient be told first that the tray has arrived. Then, move the table, carrying the food tray, to a position in front of the patient that would be reachable. - It is very important to indicate to them anything hot, like a lid on an entree, hot beverage, or soup. Then remove the lids, (letting them know where), provide a straw for the hot beverages, and remove any peel back lids on items like ice cream cups, juices, or puddings. - My father did need help with the beverages. Not being able to sit up straight, the soup spilled before he could get it into his mouth. Also a straw was required for his coffee. - Describe the location of each food item on the tray. This can be accomplished by putting a utensil, like a spoon, into their hand and guiding their hand toward the item as you explain what it is. - Most important, totally blind people don't use knifes. It is important to have any items that need cutting be done prior to the blind person eating. - My father, because of his surgery, was not able to sit up straight to take his meals. Straws were not on the trays at all. There were times when he received no help at all with some of his meals, nor did he know sometimes when they had arrived. My father deserved better in the assistance at meals. Are the volunteers trained to feed these vulnerable people who are unable to help themselves? Perhaps that would be the answer. There could be a networking system to let volunteers know when their help is required to feed a patient. Certainly I spent as much time as I could with my father when he was in the hospital. When I could not be there, I hoped that he was being helped with his meals all of the time. He enjoys his food and eating his meals would help him to get better. Please find an answer to this situation Sincerely XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, daughter Encl.

Comment: I brought my XX year old son to the Emerg department for having hives all over his body.  When we arrived, the nurse started to take his vital signs and didn't even asked why we were there.  He lifted his sleeves to take his blood pressure and said 'oh he's having an allergic reaction'.  The other nurse then asked me 'did you give him an epipen?' I said no and she said 'why didn't you give him an epipen? He could die you know? We just watched a girl die because she closed up and died in front of us because she wasn't given an epipen'.  I was really upset by her lecturing me like that and I felt the need to defend myself and say 'you didn't even ask for our story!'. I explained to the nurses that it was a slow evolving rash that didn't respond to benadryl and my son didn't have any trouble breathing or swollen lips etc. The nurse continue to lecture me about the importance of giving him the epipen.  I was horrified that she had to tell my son about seeing a young girl die.  It's not the place for her to lecture us or tell stories from previous incidents.  What the nurses don't know is that I'm a XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX at another organization.  At that moment, I was a mom first and not in the place to have to defend my decisions.  I let it go and didn't say anything but felt terrible.  The ER physician was amazing and spent time with me about what could have caused it.  The nurses during the treatment were great too.  I can tell they were busy with another patient being resuscitated but at least they treated my son and I with respect and compassion.  Suggestion for those triage nurses that evening.  Get a full history first from the account of the patient. Don't assume based on what a person looks like that they don't know what they are doing or saying.  Take both objective and subjective history and do a proper assessment. Also, don't talk about recent deaths that you witness in the ED as a tactic to scare people as a lesson. I can only imagine that being a triage nurse is not easy, but perhaps this nurse needs EAP for PTSD? She seemed angry at me for not giving the Epipen. Perhaps seeing my son with hives was a trigger for her, I don't know ... but the lecture didn't help us.   I took my son to see his allergist after and found he has new food allergies. I asked him about whether the epipen should have been given that evening and he said no,  He said that if he had no trouble breathing and no swelling etc it's not needed. He said with slow evolving hives you can't tell if it will go away with treatment or not.  In other words he said I did the right thing by taking him  to Emerg since the Benadryl didn't work.  Just wanted to highlight this because this nurse just gave wrong advice.  I have been taking my sons to this Emerg for years (probably over 30 times now) and would still recommend this site.  I'm starting to know the ER physicians and have so much trust in their care and clinical judgement. They treat patients well too.  Nurses are great except for this one nurse.

Comment: I got to the emergency, somewhere between 2300 hours and 0000 hours.  I thank the team that worked with me inside the room the next morning.  The doctor was absolutely amazing. The portion of the visit that made me very sad, was when I sat at the waiting room, after the triage nurse told me to sit and wait for my turn.  Somewhere between 0330 & 0400 hrs.  I had to go to the desk for help.  I coughed so much, and that's what got me there in the first place.  Everyone came in after me, kept going in for care, and I was just not even reassured or anything.  I was so restless and stressed to the roof.  The sitting posture, back injuries I suffered, due to a MVA in XXXXXXXXXX, and the persistent, non - productive cough, had me overstretched.  While I was not in distress, I left home in tears, in pursuit of care from the doctor.  While I sat there, the triage nurse kept going in and out the building, from the same door I entered the hospital through.  She looked in my direction many times, but appeared she just didn't see me.  If she had seen me, I presume, she would have been reminded of my presence and need for care.  I was so concerned, but did not want to be a nuisance.  However, when I could not bear it no more, I went up to the desk, and enquired of my chance to see the doctor, that's when the nurse apologized and hurriedly tried to do damage control.  When I got inside, the doctor was shocked when he discovered that I have been waiting for so long.  Even when I was leaving, the nurse showed a bit of remorse in apologizing, but I was in disbelief.  I was in shock that the hand - full of patients that visited the emergency, did not warrant me sitting there for so many hours, before seeing the care team.  Based on my observation, I think the nurse got distracted with colleagues as I have seen congregation and chattering at times.  Additionally, I strongly believe my blackness was unfortunately played a role in how the nurse saw me.  Sorry, but we usually get the 'blunt of the knife' due to perception of how less of a human we are perceived to be.  I live in the vicinity, but I pray that the right staff will be there, with the right judgment, focus, and heart, to care for me, should I need care and can't speak for myself.  I ended up seeing an allergist and respiratory therapist, due to my chronic condition.  I'll always remember walking out, and driving home, when it was day light.  I was up for the entire night and still had that terrible cough on my way.  Up all night.  Anyway, thanks for this opportunity.  I hope it never happens again after this! Comment: I knew ahead of time I needed to be admitted in the hospital due to failing kidneys. I was instructed by my Nephrologist (who works for the hospital) to proceed to the emergency department and have the staff on hand contact her upon my arrival. Despite explaining this information to the ER staff, I had to end up repeating myself over and over before my physician was finally informed. When I was finally admitted, I had to spend over six hours sitting in the waiting room until a bed became available. I understood there were no beds available at that time in the Nephrology ward, however I feel I should have been given one in the emergency department. Again, I am very understanding that a hospital tends to have long wait times and beds have become a hard thing to come by but many people who visit the emergency department is typically not in an emergency situation. Which now leads me to my next point, there should be something implemented to ensure the emergency department is not congested with nonsense (people who are not in need of urgent care). I don't want to fully suggest people get turned away however throughout the time I was in the emergency department, people with minor matters (a bee sting, a mild fever, a sore throat) came in and occupied the space and time of the attending physicians away from the genuinely ill. There was even one couple in particular that openly spoke about only coming to the emergency department because they deemed it quicker to get blood tests and ultrasounds done as opposed to going to their local clinic/laboratory. This type of behaviour and mentality is burdening the health care system and there should be a way to stop it. Maybe when people like this come in, the hospital staff should swiftly refer them to a walk-in clinic? Another area that should be assessed is the actual wards themselves. When I was finally able to get a bed in Nephrology, the other occupant in the room refused to be discharged, despite being given the green light by the physician that he was well enough to go home. Yes, he was elderly but elderly patients should be transferred to a nursing home/CCAC for secondary care and not allowed to occupy space for someone who may actually need the care. It was no wonder I needed to wait so long before getting a bed. I asked some of the staff why patients like that were able to stay despite being healthy enough for discharge, the response I got was 'many of these elderly patients don't want to leave because we do everything for them and at home, they don't have that so they want to stay'. That is ridiculous, a hospital is for the sick. Overall my experience was okay. The staff was kind and courteous however my biggest pet-peeve was the filthy bathroom in the room. I spent an entire week in that room and only once was it cleaned. Very unacceptable. It was disgusting and no one seemed to care. Every time I needed to use the bathroom, I had to venture down to the main lobby, which thankfully were kept clean.

I was taken into the OR where I delivered but it was prepped for a C-section. That being said, it was a horrific experience. There were no curtains or drapes used and I was exposed to the double doors - when I brought this up, there was nothing done to change it, I was just told that's how the OR is set up. There was quite a lot of time to speak with me as we were in there for 2 hours and planned interventions could have been discussed with me at that point. At the end, Dr. XX sent my placenta to be tested, whereas I wanted to take it home. This was a specific request I made on my birth plan, upon speaking with Dr. XX and again in the OR when I delivered it, but Dr. XX said that it was important to test it and it might impact my next child (when I'm not planning on having more children). Today, my OB said that testing the placenta wasn't necessary and that it was just procedural. I am angry that not a single thing went how I wanted including what I asked for in the moment where it wasn't medically necessary to do otherwise. I was ready to make decisions and be flexible in the moment depending on the situation, and I was, but when it came to what I wanted and what was important to me, Dr. XX did not care or listen to me. I have nothing but poor memories of the experience and would not want to recommend or return to this hospital. What is the point of asking your patients for a birth plan when it is not even discussed by the attending OB who is actually delivering let alone any part of it done even the items which are possible? I had to labor and push on my back, and was not even allowed to do so on my side. My postpartum nurse overnight checked in on me but didn't actually help - the morning nurse XXXXXX was the one who actually helped me with properly initiating breastfeeding. This person can find out the patient's status and where they are in the queue.  Waiting 8 hours without knowing what is happening, especially when you are sick and in pain, is extremely stressful patients should have a way of knowing when their turn is next.  I felt like I had been lost in the system as I still don't understand why I did not get the prescription as I was told.  I believe that a minor tweak in the system would have huge benefits for patients' well-being.  Once again, thank you very much for your compassion and all. Comment: Look. Overall, stay was okay. I know every hospital is short on budget. But here my honest feedback. Please don't get offended and I hope you take my feedback with earnesty and a desire to improve quality of care. I think the quality of service varies by each staff member. For example, during my 4 day stay, I had seen 6 nurses. Some were really good, others were not. There were inconsistent level of service due to the nature of each of the people. For example, in the first room I stayed, I was hungry and asked for a snack. The Nurse refused and said no snacks allowed at all. When I got moved to another room, I was hungry and asked for snacks, and the nurse had no problem getting me snacks. How can one nurse refuse to give snacks and another give freely? This is what I mean about the level of inconsistent care. Another example, at no point did any Doctor or Nurse explain to me the 7 types of medication I was receiving. They did give me a pamphlet, but expected me to do my own reading. I asked the first Nurse to explain my medication and each of its purpose and she just got irritated and told me 'Don't worry, just take your medication. You can read the pamphlet later.' The 2nd nurse I asked took the time to explain briefly what each medication was for. Again, why is that one Nurse didn't mind explaining the meds and another Nurse did not want to? One more thing. I was an emergency patient so I was automatically registered. At no point did anybody ask me about my dietary needs. For my first meal after surgery, I was given a meat tray. No one had asked me to know that I was a Vegetarian, but more specifically a VEGAN. I told the nurse and she tried her best to get me a Vegetarian meal but was only able to get snacks that particular day. They said the hospital DOES NOT CATER for VEGAN meals. Anyhow, I asked her to update the records to Vegetarian. I thought she did, but the next morning came another MEAT tray. The new nurse was able to get me a VEG meal at the last minute. It looked like the request for VEG meal did not go through. This is what I mean about inconsistent level of care. Why is it so hard to update the system? Another thing about the meals. About 75% of the time there was a check list or menu printed which explained what my meal was. 25% it was missing. Why is that? I feel that Dr's and Nurses generally don't like explaining anything to patients . This has been my experience during my 4 days where I saw several different Dr's and Nurses. The Dr who performed my surgery told me in 1-2 sentences about my condition and what he was doing. He did not bother to properly explain anything at all. Even when the procedure was done, he just took off and did not explain anything at all. Never heard from him ever again. The other Dr who checked on me the next day spent 2 min explaining and was in a hurry to leave. If I did not stop him and ask several questions, i would not have known much about my condition. During my 4 day stay, the room was only cleaned once and that was JUST sweeping and nothing else. Toilets were never cleaned once. Sweeping job was the worst ever. They come in and sweep in 20 seconds, missing every major spot and just leave. Again, my overall stay was OK. However, I think there is a lot of room for improvement. I used the call button in duress several times then to check with the desk, ensure the nurse received the request, and even then I had a very long wait. I know the nurse was dealing with other patients who were very demanding and in much need as well (because I could hear this going on through the hall and in adjacent rooms). No other nurses seemed to have time to help my nurse. The doors were left open at night and the floor was noisy from some very distraught patients in the area of my room. Preparing for this hospital visit and admitting myself into the hospital all happened in a very organized way. I understand that due to COVID-19, my hospital experience had to be a little more restricted (i.e. earlier discharge, having no family members for support), however I was not happy with the series of events that occurred regarding my discharge. Firstly, I was not told it was going to be a same-day discharge until AFTER my surgery. Up until my surgery, I was informed that I would stay at the hospital overnight. Therefore, I was not able to prepare myself beforehand to be discharged that day. I was also in a serious amount of pain and taking a lot of pain medications, therefore I was not able to think clearly. The nurses and physician assistant (I'm not sure if it was the physician assistant or someone else) told me I had to be discharged early while I was still feeling a lot of pain and feeling lightheaded to a point where I almost felt unconscious. I understand that I had to be discharged, but I was not able to fully understand the other things they were telling me regarding my discharge, due to the state I was in. They were able to speak to my daughter over the phone and inform her about the discharge, but even then, she stated that the conversation was rushed and she was not able to clarify important things. When I was discharged, someone packed all my things in a bag and tried to explain things to me that I had to do, but I was feeling too lightheaded to a point where I was not able to fully understand and process what was being said. They brought my in a wheelchair and left me outside in the parking lot when it was cold and dark until my daughter and husband came to pick me up. I was outside by the parking lot for 45 minutes all alone, in a lot of pain, and feeling unconscious with no one by my side. This made me feel very upset and if I had known that this was how my discharge was going to be, I would not have chosen to do my elective surgery at this time. I suggest that if this is the case, have someone contact a family member after discharge to ensure that the patient is safe and all their questions have been answered. (This response was not meant to offend anyone and I apologize if it did. Overall, I am still satisfied and grateful to have my surgery done and I am happy that the surgery all happened safely as I am now recovering very well. This response was a part of the patient experience that I wanted to share.)
