Compliment:  During the course of this stay at XXXXXXXXX, my son and I have experienced the following:  1) Communication between teams regarding my son is thorough and information regarding his condition that has went unacknowledged and/or unknown at other hospitals, is recorded and reported between team members. The nurses and IV team are knowledgeable about my son's condition, history and needs in a detailed way,  2) Tests ordered and carried out quickly,  3) Clear plans are made in preparation for various outcomes (airway at bedside, close observation following anaesthesia) with patient safety as a priority,  4) Nursing staff are thorough, present and seem to truly care about my son, 5) Dialogue between nursing staff within earshot of parents, is appropriate, considerate and professional,  6) There is an emphasis on making a plan of care and keeping parents informed as the plan evolves,  7) Discharge papers are exceptionally thorough. I am very grateful for the expertise, experience and medical care that is available there. 8) Our neurosurgeon's care, professionalism and attention to detail are second to none. I knew my son was in the best hands possible,  Concern: I have concerns with the lack of communication surrounding the process and role of parents in Observation room XXXX as well as the accommodations provided for them. Parents are usually expected to do the bedside care in the private rooms, however, once a child is moved into observation the expectation is unclear. Services and accommodations are not explained and the space is tight quarters. I was not told until 8pm on my son's second day there that we wouldn't be moved out of that room after being told that morning that we would be. At that point, my options were limited. The nurse told me that if it were earlier, I could have tried for a room at XXX which had never been offered- not helpful. An upright chair to sleep bedside again? A hotel in the middle of the third wave of a pandemic and provincial lockdown? Parents are already putting aside their own needs and prioritizing their child (holding for positional X-rays, bloodwork, IV's, waiting for MRI's and CT's etc.) on top of the emotional aspect of having a child we are worried about. They need to be able to address their basic needs-- food, water, shower, sleep. Shower and sleep are a problem in the observation room and since there are only 4 beds in there, it seems easy to replace the upright chairs with reclining ones without getting in the way of nurse access or encroaching on other bed areas. I watched a tired mom come in with her infant, rarely leave the room and sleep upright for 2 nights. I took my sheets and pillow and slept on a park bench in the main hallway because I could not sleep upright another night, having had previous back injuries. The woman was still there when I left. I believe there needs to be more communication with parents regarding this room. Upright chairs that were previously chosen to deter parents from staying overnight need to be reconsidered given the pandemic.  ** It would be helpful for parents to have someone/a volunteer give them an orientation when they enter any unit. On our most recent visit (this week) my son was in the PICU and one of the nurses explained in detail my options and provided me with clear directions to services and facilities that were available to me. This was so helpful and had me feeling like a valuable member of the care team.   Additionally, someone to do a brief orientation of the unit with parents upon arrival would be very helpful (food process for patients, kitchen, Ronald McDonald room) etc. Medical information and test appts can be overwhelming and a bit disarming so having these pieces taken care of from the beginning would help.  Thank you for seeking parent feedback.

Comment: From attachment - XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX My daughter was scheduled for surgery on phone by one of the XXXXXXXXX personnel.  No pre-surgery information/instructions of what to do before arriving to the hospital was given, except the Covid-19 test on the child and some blood work.  Arriving in the hospital on that faithful day, while preparing for the surgery, the surgeon team gave me a consent form to sign and said that the rod they will use during the surgery to correct my daughter's spinal code will be the traditional type.  I told the team that the lead doctor, my husband, and I discussed this with him last time we visited the hospital, that using the traditional rode will subject our daughter to nothing less than fourteen surgeries before she turned 14 yrs of age.  The same lead doctor was the one that suggested the options for us to choose but said that he can only use the magnetic rod on her if only we can work on her behavior to ensure she lies down stably during the rod stretching which will occur on every six months period after the surgery.  We also suggested if anesthesia can be used to induce her during the magnetic rod stretching process as it's the same drug, they will still use on her, each and every surgery, every sic months until she turns fourteen if the traditional rod is used.  That was almost 12 months before the surgery date.  Since then we have been working so hard towards our daughter's behavior and she had drastically improved in so many ways, only to arrive in the hospital on the day of surgery to discover a new development without prior notice.  No one informed us of any reason or why a sudden change of mind by the lead doctor to use the traditional rod, when the option to use the magnetic type is available, which will require one or two surgeries in the process instead of about fifteen surgeries for the next seven years, for a little child with autism, Soto Syndrome, speech delay and Global delay.  The team told me, there's nothing they can do as they are acting on instruction giving to them by the lead doctor.  The team suggested calling the lead doctor to speak with me.  When the lead doctor came; he said, he has already decided to use the traditional rod on her.  It's either we accept it or nothing and that we can forget about XXXXXXXXX and go somewhere else.  He did not even want to hear a word from me rather he screamed at me and said, it's either we accept his decision or go home, and he walked away.  I requested the team to call XXXXX's father to inform him of what the lead doctor said.  As he came with us to the hospital but was not allowed to check-in due to the Covid-19 restriction.  He was waiting outside because only one parent was allowed to check-in with the child.  When I called XXXXX's father he requested to talk to one of th team members.  And the doctor he was talking to, said that the decision was not in his position to make and that they are acting on instruction.  XXXXX's dad requested to speak with the lead doctor but he completely but he wasn't there any longer.  We requested to find out why he did not want to use the magnetic rod for the surgery even when our daughter's behavioral stability has noticeably improved, but no answer was given.  A few months later the Orthopedic of XXXXXXXXX scheduled an appointment to see XXXXX.  When I got there, the doctor asked me why XXXXX did not go through surgery scheduled for her?  I explained the whole story to him.  He said, well!  He doesn't think we have any other choice for the option given to us.  He repeated the same word the lead doctor used, "it's either we accept the option of the traditional rod or nothing"  The way he spoke to me in a dissented way, sounded like a complicity or someone with a prearranged response waiting for arrival to his office.  He even went his way to mockingly told me to my face that he has three children who are diagnosed with Soto's syndrome  The way he said it, suggested some level of derision to my daugr's situation, which's hardly expected from a medical practitioner at his level.  I already knew the condition of my daughter and do not need to be reminded of it or to be mocked about it by the same medical practitioner who supposed to encouragingly assist her condition in any way he can.  He also told me if we do not accept the use of traditional rod on our child, that we should not bother bringing her to XXXXXXXXX any longer and we should find somewhere else.  I was very devastated and very sad to hear such words from a medical doctor.  His behavior towards my daughter and I in his office got me very scared and I'm still very scared to continue to confide my daughter's situation in their care.  I have complexly lost trust in the way my daughter and I were treated.  It's like my daughter's wellbeing does not really matter, probably, as a result of her racial background.

Comment: I am always grateful to live in the same city as XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX as I believe it is a world class institution for children's health.  I was appreciative of the high quality of care and attention paid to my daughter by everyone she interacted with during her visit to the ER department this time.  My only comment for potential improvement was the lack of visibility over the length of time it took to complete the visit.  While I have no medical background, I am familiar enough with triage to know that this was a function of how many other patients were in the ER at that time and the relative severity of my daughter's injury compared with what the other children were there for.  It may be impossible, but if there was some way to give parents a sense of the overall steps in the process and likely time associated with each step, this could help manage expectations around wait times from the outset.  The screens around the ER with patient volumes and general wait times were somewhat helpful, but bringing it down to the specifics for the patient would be even better.  For example - the triage nurse could say, 'You're here for a injury and possible broken bone.  First step is an x-ray.  That will likely take xx minutes to arrange and get through.  We'll want that x-ray reviewed by our ER doctor and probably someone from orthopedics.  That will likely take another xx minutes, given how busy we are.  Depending on the results of that x-ray, you may need further treatment like a cast or splint, which will be maybe another xx minutes.'  That would help me as a parent figure out whether to get my daughter a snack, call my wife to drop off more entertainment / book, etc.  I'm sure it is difficult to lay out a potential roadmap of the path through the ER based solely on the brief visit with the triage nurse, but for something relatively straightforward like my daughter's injury, it may be possible / helpful to parents.   I also wanted to thank the nurse who tracked down a loaner cell phone charger for my daughter's phone.  In my haste to get to the hospital, I didn't bring one and didn't realize my daughter's phone was low on battery.  Having access to her screen helped her (and thus me) pass the time.  This is certainly not a 'service' I would expect at a hospital, but it was an act of kindness by a nurse who I'm sure had more important things to do at the time.  I really appreciated it.  Thank you also to all of the XXXXXXXX staff who are working hard in normal times, but during this period of additional stress and complexity with COVID have been going even more above and beyond.  Your contribution to the health of our children and the well-being of our city (and beyond) is extremely important and often under acknowledged.  THANK YOU!!!

I have 3 concerns about this hospital stay.  1. While my daughter and I were in the ED, the doctors involved in her care had a lengthy email debate about which department should admit her as a patient. This debate went on overnight for many hours, while I waited in the ED without an update. When the update finally came, around 4:30 am, it was that I would need to wait in the ED for an indefinite period, as the department to which my daughter had been transferred did not have any beds available. By that point, I knew we were in for a stay of at least a few days' duration, so I thought this could not possibly be true. However, no other solutions were offered, at least until I, pretty forcefully, objected - under the COVID rules at the time, I would not be permitted to leave the ED to get food, I couldn't switch with my husband, and there was nowhere for me to sleep. Folks. A patient's care plan should not involve, as your first option, an indefinite stay in a department that doesn't permit the patient's caregiver to access food or sleep. Very luckily for me, a room was found about an hour after I raised my concerns. I appreciate that there are probably all sorts of difficulties with finding a bed/nurse on short notice. However, one was found very quickly after I complained - why wasn't finding this alternative bed the first option?    2. During her stay, my daughter required IV antibiotics. She was quite active and the IV fell out or was pulled out by her many times. The IV team usually came quickly to insert a new IV. On one occasion, however, the IV team was called but was unable to come for a few hours, so a nurse from another floor was sent. This nurse poked my daughter three times unsuccessfully. We were not in any danger of missing the time to administer her dose and I was not advocating for a faster IV insertion. I have no idea why this happened and it caused my daughter unnecessary distress.   3. Initially, my daughter was to receive IV antibiotics for two weeks. The plan was to insert a picc line, send her home, and arrange for home care nursing to deliver the antibiotics via pump. The picc line was inserted, but there were no home care nurses available over the XXXXXXXXX/XXXXXXXX holidays to administer her medicine. The discharge planning team suggested instead that we use an alternative pump, that we could be trained to use ourselves (I think someone referred to it as a balloon at some point), but when they looked into it, they found that her dose was too small to be administered this way. Because these two options were off the table, it was decided, after a consultation with infectious disease, that she could be given an oral antibiotic instead. I said at the time that this was a smart solution, and I still believe that to be the case. However, could it not be anticipated that home care nursing would not be available over the holidays, especially during the COVID pandemic? Could the consultation with infectious disease not have taken place prior to the picc insertion, perhaps with the knowledge that home care nursing might be unavailable? Because of a blood clot formed when an earlier picc line was in place (when she was born at 25 weeks' gestation), she required enoxaparin while this second picc line was in. I understand it's difficult to anticipate the twists and turns that might arise when administering complicated medical care - but could these things truly not be anticipated? Was there no way to avoid administering a blood thinner to maintain an arguably unnecessary picc line? I do wonder.   I think it's worth noting here that, notwithstanding the above, the vast majority of my interactions with the health care providers at XXXXXXXXX have been professional and respectful, and it is obvious that these are very knowledgeable and competent people who care about my kid. I will forever be appreciative of the care she has received during this stay, as well as during previous stays (hoping to avoid future stays!). T said, nothing is perfect 100% of the time and there's usually always room to improve.

Comment: I was very disappointed about this experience. I felt intimidated by my son's end doctor (we were bounced around from room to room for a few hours and the wound was not cleaned during this time) and I do not feel that she was honest with me.  This doctor had recommended stitches, given the depth and nature of the wound. I had requested that a plastic surgeon assist with the wound close since it was on his face. My brother in law is a plastic surgeon in South Africa and had recommended this approach. I'd indicated that I had private medical aid which could cover this and that this was important to me, and that I'd even be willing to cover this myself if needs be. The doctor said that this would take some additional wait time. I'd indicated an extra bit of wait time would be okay as long as wasn't too much longer as we'd already been there for some time. She said she'd get back to me. I didn't see her again for 2 hours. I asked the nurse if she'd be coming back and she said she'd look into it. Finally the doctor  came back in. She indicated that if I wanted a plastic surgeon I'd be responsible for additional trauma to my son (and would I really want to be responsible for this? ). She said that he would need to wait several more hours, that he would need to go under general anesthesia and have tubes stuck down his throat and would waste hospital time and nurse time as 2 additional nurses would be needed. I'm not quite sure where the difference would be between her stitching the wound or a plastic surgeon? Why would this extra step be needed? This was very intimidating for me. She then left and came back 30 min later saying she'd decided that surgical glue would be the best approach since if we waited any longer the risk of infection would be high. I felt as though she was just trying to get rid of us by this change of medical opinion but said that if she felt that this was honestly the best approach that I would respect her medical opinion. She left again. After 45 min I asked the nurses if she'd be coming back and if anyone was going to take his pulse and a few other things the doctor had indicated were needed. Eventually they came back, woke my now sleeping child to medicine up his nose for the pain, cleaned and sealed the wound. They then left, my son started to have an allergic reaction to the bandages so I called a nurse and asked her to assist, she said she'd call the doctor . I could hear the doctor talking to the nurse in the passage saying that she didn't want to come back into the room and the nurse insisting that she tend to the issue. They came back in, removed the surgical strips, told me if it were to open then just to leave it to close naturally and that more severe scarring could be expected. We left the hospital about 30 min later. All in all we had driven from XXXXXXX at 12 am, arrived at the hospital at 1 pm, only received treatment at 8:50 pm, and were discharged at 9:30 pm. During this entire time my X year old was not allowed to eat or drink anything where the last thing he'd had to drink and eat was at 10 am. There was no accessible water for me either. We came to XXXXXXXXX because we knew we'd get the best treatment and trust me, I fully understand and appreciate the amazing efforts of the nurses and doctors during this epidemic. My family is full of medical doctors so I fully know the challenges which doctors face. I really feel, however, that this particular doctor needs significant work on their bedside manner and I don't appreciate feeling intimidated and lied to.

I would review with the doctors and x ray techs the proper positioning of knees when x raying for OCD and also encourage doctors to not be as skeptical of information parents are giving them, especially when they bring in records of MRI's etc - might be of value to actually look at the paperwork if there's new pain involved with areas that have shown fractures on MRI.    Before my son was xrayed, the doctor told us he wouldn't be standing if it was fractured which is not true of OCD fractures -  most kids can actually walk, run, etc with this type of fracture but it will cause pain.  Even if you don't believe parents you can interact with empathy as most parents who come to emerg would rather be anywhere else but there, but are obviously worried or anxious.  We let the doctor know that we had just found out less than a week before that both knees were showing fracture lines on both condyles and we were waiting on a reading of an MRI to confirm the degree.  We were still in a state of disbelief as they seemed to be happening and some healing without any symptoms,   My son had new lateral knee pain and we had just had OCDs confirmed by X-ray less than a week before - we were waiting to hear whether or not the lateral one was fully healed so new pain in that location concerned me.  The emerg doctor agreed to X-ray, which I appreciated and afterwards he told us there was no new fracture and that our son actually didn't have any fractures in the knee.  When I asked our sports doctor about this I was told that there are specific techniques to x-raying for OCD that allows for better views of this type of fracture - not sure if the doctor has to request this?  Fortunately this lateral knee pain was not a worsening of the fracture and as we were referred two weeks later to ortho by our sports doctor, the care is being managed - our son continues to remain on very limited activity as these types of fractures take months and months to heal and he will have a followup MRI in XXXX.  I have no intention of this letter being one of criticism but more informative than anything - I was impressed by all staff and was expecting it to be more intimidating because it is the renowned XXXXXXXXX hospital - I think XXX received good care and appreciate that OCDs, hence the info I provided above is only meant to be that- just some info to consider in terms of management and interactions.  Thanks again, XXXXXXXX

Our visit to the emergency room took 21.5 hours from start to finish. I also did not bring a cell phone charger, thinking that we wouldn't be at the hospital for very long, so I was disappointed to not be able to find publicly available chargers, as I've found at another hospital that we normally use.  Overall, I felt that most of the communications between the hospital staff and myself were lackin I was not informed clearly of how severe the broken bone was, and only understood after I got home and did research on it.  However, there were a few nurses who were very compassionate and caring, and I'm appreciative of their care.  Unfortunately, this was quite inconsistent.  And for the most part, we felt forgotten for many hours.  After this experience, I would hesitate to return to XXXXXXXXX for an emergency, and would not recommend others to go there with their children unless absolutely necessary.

Comment: My son came in with an issue creating discomfort on XXXXXX.   We arrived at approximately 10:30 am and left at 9 pm.     The triage was quick and we were placed in an area where the nurse and doctor were attentive.    After about 1.5 hours of process,  where we were told an ultrasound was required, we then proceeded to wait for 3 hours for any follow up of any kind, which I had to initiate. We called the on call nurse on multiple occasions to ask for an update and received a quick reply that they were looking into it.  During that time my son had not eaten or drank anything since 8 am.  I explained this to the call nurse at least twice as I waited for an update.  Now about 3:30 pm I finally asked the call nurse to get someone to come visit our room, which the nurse did.  It was at that point it was revealed that there had in fact been no prohibition ok good or drink and that I was free to get some for my son who had been complaining for hours. The nurse, feeling bad, procured easily accessible juice and cookies that had been there the whole time for us to take and then did vitals - though I note that four hours had based before his previous ones.   After 5.5 hours of total wait from when we saw the doctor, 7 hours total, we were taken to an ultrasound where a resident performed it.  He did his best but a X year old child presents challenges.  He completed the ultrasound but came back afterwards to do more because of imagining and a failure to take a measurement.  The fellow then came back to perform her own a separate scan.  This took another 1.2 hours total, for an ultrasound of the abdomen, kidneys and groin/testicles.  After that we were told we would be transported back to emergency.  But no one came. Another 30 of waiting before the resident came back and asked if anyone was told to come get you. I said no. He said he'd make another call.   We finally went down to emergency and waited another 2 hours before being discharged.  Despite the further wait, we asked new nurse and the staff doctor separately if they could give us a sense of whether we needed to wait or if we could get food. The same thing happened earlier but my son was given cookies to placate his hunger. Now 5 hours later we were back in the same position asking for approval to leave to eat. My son is X years old. As a parent, anyone would appreciate that I can't have him go through the day on a diet of cookies and apple juice.  Again it seemed I had the sympathy of the staff, but not enough responsiveness in what I could do.  So we just kept waiting before finally leaving at 10:30 pm.  Before I get to the point, there are two important facts I want to share before I offer my view on this 12 hour experience.  First, I am a XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX who has previously represented doctors and nurses in complaints before their respective colleges. I am aware of the standards that apply and the care required.    Second, I am also unfortunately not new to the hospital system.  This same son is a survivor of a childhood cancer and we have gotten well acquainted with XXXXXXXXX and it's phenomenal oncology group.    With that all in mind, along with the personal affection and gratitude I have for this hospital, I have to say that today was just a completely inexcusable experience. While a long wait time is often expected when you go to a hospital, particularly through emergency, the lack of transparency, reporting, diligence and care to ensuring that patients don't have to be their own best advocates - particularly for simple things like food and water - is far below the standard I would expect of and understand is required of this hospital.  Being left uncared for for hours or left in a dark room waiting transport are also things I'd say fall below the standard.    While everyone we encountered was apologetic at the missed connections that ultimately resulted in our day being taken through today's process - the doctor, nurse, ultrasound fellow, the radiologist, staff dor and the transporter - it doesn't make up for the indifference my son or I felt each time those involved likely thought we were complaining.  It was also a fundamentally disappointing experience to find every person helping us leave for the day when we probably and could have been out much sooner.   We are all busy professionals but the expectation held by the society we serve is that we stay professional as we are held to that strict standard. Today missed the mark and while likely isolated isn't any less warranted of a complaint as I'd expect of any client of mine with whom I failed to be responsive, transparent, or diligent with.
Code: Access/Coord of Care, Admit/Registration, Dietary/Service, Doctor/Physician, Emergency Dept, Information/Education, Nurse/Nurse aide, Physical Comfort, Radiology

My XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX son was seen at the ER for an asthma exacerbation on XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. He had recently come to the ER just 17 days earlier for an asthma exacerbation, was admitted, and spent 4 days as an inpatient. He had also spent 4 days as an inpatient at XXXXXX hospital before coming to XXXXXXXXX, and had rebounded after discharge from Humber. The staff doctor, Dr. XXXXXXX had been very attentive, concerned, and empathetic during the previous ER visit (XXXXXXXXXXXX).   On this second visit (XXXXXXXXXX) my son was also receiving care from Dr. XXXXXXX, who did not remember the previous visit (fair enough, he sees a lot of patients). My son did receive rapid and appropriate care. He responded well to the medications and began to feel much better after a couple of hours.   This relatively rapid turnaround raised Dr. XXXXXXX's skepticism, that some of the symptoms my son had experienced that led to his coming to the ER were from anxiety, and he ordered a pulmonary function test which confirmed that my son's breathing was doing well. This also confirmed Dr. XXXXXXX's suspicions that anxiety was involved in this particular presentation. I was aware of the interplay of anxiety and asthma, and I was also aware that my son had just recently gone through a very frightening asthma exacerbation and naturally we would be worried about any perceived difficulties breathing.   Our son also has a diagnosed anxiety disorder for which he is followed by excellent mental health professionals, and we are forthright in disclosing this history with his medical team, and had certainly shared that history on this ER visit.  My issue is that the way in which Dr. XXXXXXXX communicated his concerns left my son, and my husband and me, feeling very negatively about this ER visit. With respect to his finding that anxiety was a contributing factor, Dr. XXXXXXX did not speak directly, nor empathetically to our son, but rather spoke over him to my husband and I, explaining how he had solved this case. He did not engage our son in a discussion about how scary asthma is, or how he had just been through a difficult experience (having suddenly experienced a severe acute asthma exacerbation weeks earlier, involving 4 ER visits and two hospital admissions) and how it will take time to learn to manage this condition, and recognize when anxiety may be a factor in his symptoms and in managing a flare. We felt more like we had been scolded and that we were judged to be naive and were 'overmedicalizing'. Nonetheless, Dr. XXXXXXX was professional and we were given appropriate discharge instructions, including instructions for managing this exacerbation with asthma medication over the next couple of days. Upon leaving the ER, my son was upset. He felt shamed and guilty, and repeated that his asthma wasn't real and was just from 'anxiety': that was the message he heard, that was his 'takeaway'.  Although I don't believe it was his intention to make us feel negatively, we perceived that Dr. XXXXXXX used an admonishing tone and style to discuss his diagnosis, which was insensitive to both my son, and my husband and me. Since this visit, my son returned to the ER in late XXXXXXXX, when he experienced an asthma exacerbation that was triggered by being exposed to ammonia fumes at school. He was treated quickly, and respectfully, and he responded well to the medications and was able to be discharged home after six hours. We followed up with his respirologist the next day: his pulmonary function tests were very poor, and we continued to treat him with medication over the next few days until he had appropriate improvement. We do not have good control over his asthma and he is starting injectable biologic therapy with Xolair shortly with hopes for improvement. My hope in writing this story, is that ER staff will continue to be educated about sensitive and empathetic patient communication, so that they can be a positive voice in a patient's progression towards managing illne Even though ER staff only have a short time to spend with patients, their words and attitude have a significant impact on each patient they see.
Code: Access/Coord of Care, Continuity/Transition, Discharge, Doctor/Physician, Emergency Dept, Emotional Support, Information/Education, Medication/Prescrip, Respect to Patient, Positive Recognition

Comment: The visit started during the business hours 9-5 pm, 10 am specifically and we did not leave the hospital until 7 pm due to how the discharge worked.  We were advised by the nurse that we were next to be seen by the doctor around 11:15 am, but the doctor showed up at 1:45 pm.  That is a 2 hour wait for a person that was next.  The patient was a baby and it was only myself and him.  We were not able to leave the waiting room to get food or anything as if we did, we may have missed the doctor.  This is a fundamental problem for cases where the patient has only one guardian at the hospital as once we enter the waiting rooms, we cannot leave to get anything, ie food.  The baby had a potential fractured wrist and was not treated any faster then any other patient who did not have this or a lesser condition.  I recommend that age be a factor to how urgent care someone should be seen as babies do not have patience and are more susceptible to getting sick with a weaker immune system.  Being stuck in the room where the baby cannot move as the facility has dangerous machinery or items around is unsafe.  We were not sick when we went, but after spending over 8 hours in emergency care where sick people go, it makes the potential of healthy people getting sick which should be prevented.  We saw other patients who came in later get discharged earlier when our baby did not get any care.  It appeared that older children were seen first who may or may not have had a serious reason to be there as they were discharged earlier in comparison to the baby.  We got a new doctor at the end that explained the condition and what was required next and said that they would set up an appointment with the plastic doctor at 4:45 pm.  There was nothing else required.  We then waited 2+ hours before we could leave as we did not receive any discharge papers.  I asked a couple of times at the front desk if they could call me when an appointment was set up as it made no sense to have my baby stay any longer then the 6 hrs he did already to wait for an appointment.  This can be done via a phone call.  The front desk said we could not leave until we got our discharge papers and the doctors was not around so we waited and waited for 2+ hours to get some papers and an appointment.  There should be no reason to hold us longer for this as it could be done via a phone call.  And the discharge papers should have been given at the time of the diagnosis so that there is no time wasted for both people.  I understand if there was a serious condition where waiting was required, but for this there was no reason to force us to wait 2 more hours to finish from an already long wait.  This process needs to be improved to be more efficiently done for the patients and doctors,whether the write up of the discharge papers are done by someone else so that the doctor can attend other patients could be a solution.

The triage nurse impatiently told us that it takes 3 days for antibiotics to work and suggested we should not be there. When we saw a resident, she said the infection should have responded within 2 days, and she didn't think this was the right diagnosis. She wanted to get a urine sample by catheter to test for a UTI.   We expressed concern about the method the nurse planned to use because our son is uncircumcised, and my wife had read a paper in a medical journal indicating that retracting the foreskins of very young boys can cause injury. The paper described a method for catheterization that did not involve retracting the foreskin. The resident said nobody at XXXXXXXXX would be able to use that method. My wife said that we would prefer to take our son home and discuss the issue with our family doctor, a very experienced physician with the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX team, before continuing with the test. The resident confirmed that our son would not be at any risk if we waited a day or two and got some advice, but only after she laughed at our concern and said 'There is no difference of opinion about this', and told us the nurse had been using the same method for XX years.   Later in the week when our son's symptoms had not resolved, we ended up going to XXXXXXXXXXXXXX hospital's pediatric ER. The attending there told us that since our son was already taking antibiotics for the suspected ear infection, finding out whether he had a UTI would not change the course of treatment so this invasive test was unnecessary.   This was the first time we had been to XXXXXXXXX and overall it was a pretty disappointing experience. Both the doctors who examined our son were rushed and not very gentle in their examinations. One of them really hurt his ear while looking inside it. Nobody talked to him about what they were going to do before doing it, although he is old enough to understand many things that are said to him. Of course everyone has many patients to see, but it only takes a few seconds to make eye contact with a child and treat them like a person. The staff at XXXXXXXXXXXXXX were much more patient and friendly and took more time with their examinations, and were more responsive to our concerns about the test that was proposed at XXXXXXXXX. The contrast was really striking.

I am so glad to be completing this survey as it gives me the opportunity to share how a traumatic experience become a wonderful experience, one where all workers demonstrated such high levels of skill sets, attention to detail, care, passion, and Professionalism. And we were also given a small hat for our newborn to wear (heart felt gift and appreciative as the hat we had brought did not fit her). Comment: From Attachment - XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  Re: Survey from XXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXX  Hospital stay at XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.  I am happy to provide you with my experience at XXXXXXXXX.  To begin I have Multiple Myeloma and I am presently in a Clinical Trial at XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX under the care of Dr. XXXXXXXXXXX, awaiting a transplant.  Also let me begin that the XXXXXXXXXXX family are big supporters of hospitals and this can be easily verified.  At the end of XXXXXXXX I became ill with vomiting, diarrhea and developed a fever.  We contacted XXX and were advised to go to Emergency, they thought XXXXXXXXX could work as they have a good Oncology dept. and so because it was much closer for us that's where we went.  When we got there we were told I had to be admitted.  There were no beds available so I spent two nights in the Emergency.  By the way the nurses in Emergency were wonderful.  I was eventually moved, to I believe was the third floor.  Upon entering I was immediately appalled that I was sharing a room with two men.  This room had paint peeling from the walls and exposing the drywall.  Immediately to my left was a dying man, who was restrained in the bed, he screamed day and night.  He would remove all his clothing and do all his business in the bed.  You can just imagine the lack of hygiene and the smells emanating from him until the nurses decided to check on him.  At one point I rang the bell on his behalf.  He would tear at the curtain that was suppose to provide some level of privacy.  My stay at XXXXXXXXX was a nightmare.  My husband pleaded to be moved especially because I was more of a cancer patient.  The answer was always the same, no beds.  I forgot to mention that there was no ho water in the taps.  When I asked the nurse how I was supposed to wash up I was handed WIPES.  I think this matter should be reported to Public Health, it is totally unacceptable.  My husband also notice that there was quite a large him or rehab room, which was always empty, these patients are almost bedridden, why would they need a gym?  How about make room for more beds and if they need rehab, I am sure there are other places for that.  The hospital stay at XXXXXXXXX has left me traumatized.  I did not feel like I was in a Canadian hospital but rather some remote clinic in Mexico somewhere.  Needless to say we were happy to leave early and continue my antibiotic treatment in the comfort of our home.  I hope that this information I have provided can bring some serious changes at your hospital, because whoever is running things now has no clue.  Sincerely XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX

The blood tech took blood from my roommate instead of me - obviously didn't check her wristband or ask the patient her name.  Medication was prescribed to me based on her bloodwork - my nurses kept asking me about having rheumatoid arthritis, internal bleeding, and other things that were completely new to me, and I kept asking questions about why I was being prescribed something new based on updated bloodwork (that I didn't have done) ... I kept insisting that I hadn't had any blood drawn in two days.  It was then that they figured out what had happened and finally someone was sent in to take my blood - and carefully checked my wristband, my name, and asked me my birthdate.  Luckily, it was only potassium that I was given based on the other woman's bloodwork (and as it was my own bloodwork indicated low potassium, so it all worked out in the end). It could have had very different consequences.  2. The other thing that made me uncomfortable during my stay was having a male roommate.  My second roommate during my stay was an older gentleman.  He was not permitted to use the washroom in our room - it sounds like it was because they were taking extra precautions with me (I had the droplet precaution sign posted and everyone had to be gowned and gloved and masked to see me).  So, the man never came into my side of the room.  However, this man happened to have a colostomy bag that needed changing every hour.  My concern was that the containers that were used to empty the colostomy bag were left on the window ledge, floor, and sink area in the washroom, emptied but not cleaned (very visible remnants coated the clear containers).  The smell was terrible, and the practice was very unsanitary.  The man also had a container for urinating in on his side of the room.  I was not comfortable using the washroom with those containers lying around.  After a particularly difficult night, I was visibly upset and crying when my doctor came in the morning. Comment: One of the worst experiences of my entire lie horrible.  I felt like I (and my mother) were in a 3rd world country care was horrible, people were nasty I'm planning on writing an editorial on this experience  From Attachment - XXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  To Whom It May Concern  In XXXX of XXXX I was called to XXXXXX to see mother (XXXXXXXXXXXX) who was not feeling well.  When I arrived she was dizzy, confused and had been falling.  After a day of being with her I brought her to XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX around 5 pm.  We sat in that waiting room until 10 pm before seeing a doctor.  While we waited I witnessed a woman vomiting so severely that she would pass out and then recover briefly then pass out again.  She was completely ignored by doctors and nurses walking by her.  At one point I thought she had died.  We went from room to room getting required tests.  They lost my mothers chart 3 times and had us waiting for hours in the wrong room twice.  I have never in my life seen such a horrific scene in any hospital in my life.  People were walking around holding up there I.V. bags, people were lined up in the halls some crying out in pain while young children ran around them.  My mother was admitted to the hospital at around 1 am. I left the hospital at 2 am.  She spent the night in the emergency room on a gurney.  No beds or rooms were available.  When I returned in the morning she was still in the ER and around 3 pm she was finally placed in a room with a older man with severe emotional issues.  He screamed at the top of his lungs for hours on end being ignored by staff.  Occasionally when he took off his clothes he would get there attention or when he threw his food tray on the floor.  He spent his days often strapped into his wheel chair in the hall or in front of our door.  Naturally with all his screaming going on my mother was not able to rest and we both found him frightening and distressing.  I asked repeatedly to have my mother moved and the answer was always NO.  I was asked to wear a gown and gloves.  It was not fully explained to me why, only that I could contaminate the nurses station if I didn't change it every time I went in and out of my mother's room.  I was reprimanded several times for stepping out the door looking for help for my mother.  My mother was tested for Mercer.  I was not given the results until it was forced upon me to take my mother out of the hospital  It turned out she did NOT have it.  The gentleman however that she shared the room with DID have it.  So why was this man in the halls of the hospital and why was my mother in the same room with him?  Finally someone decided it wasn't a good idea for him to be in the hall because he was highly contagious.  My mother had been sharing the same bathroom with this man for over 2 weeks.  She may have gotten it from him which could have contributed to her illness, but I was never informed even when she was tested a second time.  I was then instructed by the flow nurse that my mother was not eligible to stay in the hospital until we were able to find her a suitable nursing home.  The flow nurse on the weekend had assured me she would be able to stay.  I was told she would be put on top of the list, due to her current health issues (and at the age of XX) which included congestive heart failure, dementia and the list goes on and on.  I filled out multiple home placement formes and had no idea how I was going to be able to take care of her.  NO ONE cared.  I have been an XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX citizen for XX years and I live in XXXXXXXXXXXXX.  My mother was not able to immigrate to the XX as we had hoped.  For many years we tried.  She spent 6 mos. in the XX and 6 in XXXXXX.  Unfortuntely my bother died 3 years ago, with whom she was forced to live alone in a senior housing apartment. I was informed by the Flow nurse that my mother was my responsibility and that she would need to return to her apartment.  Wh was not completely out of the question as she lived there alone.  I was not comfortable in her present state for her to be on her own.  I was offered NO help as far as finding her a place to live.  I could not legally bring her to XXXXXXX, and I could not legally stay in XXXXXX.  I was told to hire a private nurse at a cost of approximately $800.00 per week.  An impossible amount for myself or my mother to afford.  I explained this to the flow nurse over and over but got nowhere.  I was often brought to tears with the hopelessness I felt, and the lack of caring or understanding of my situation from her.  I was finally forced to find a private assisted living facility in XXXXXXX.  I picked my mother u from the hospital and took her to this facility as I had absolutely NO CHOICE.  My mother was sill in a very weak state and in hind site should have stayed in the hospital.  They made it very clear she needed to leave.  Unfortunately this chain of events lead to my mothers death.  I have to say I'm horrified at the care she received in the hospital.  If I hadn't been in her room every day she probably would have died sooner.  3 to 4 nurses at at time would often help my mothers room mate, and barely make eye contact with us in hopes we would not ask for help.  I was treated with hostility, and felt hatred from some of the staff.  Someone decided it was time for my mother to see a priest.  He was there when I arrive and of course I immediately thought my mother was dying.  Neither my mother or myself had requested a priest.  I hope this letter helps someone else.  I hope that no one has to go though what we went though at XXXXXXXXX Hospital.  I hope the powers that be take this letter seriously and look into an extremely flawed hospital.  THis hospital has serious dangerous workings.  The staff are overworked and the care is horrific.  I wish I could have brought my mother back to XXXXXXX with me.  I may not have lost her.  Sincerely XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXX

I only visited the Emergency Room at the hospital since the Walk in Clinic near my home closed at 8PM.  I was 99.9% certain that all I needed was an antibiotic in lieu of an infection that I developed and did not want to go through the night without meds in an attempt to catch the infection early and prevent it from worsening. Turns out I was correct.  Truth be told, I feel the issue with the Emergency Room at the hospital is ...... too many people coming in without life threatening issues.  A BIG # of visits could totally be avoided if there were 24 hour walk in clinic or urgent care clinics or fracture clinics.  Heart attacks, strokes, kidney stones, severe unexplainable pain, injury that has led to possible internal bleeding, fevers that exceed 41 degrees, babies and infants with issues, etc., these are a handful of examples of medical issues that I feel requires hospital emergency care/visits.  The bulk of the patients I saw in the emergency ward on the evening I attended - kids having respiratory issues due to colds and flu like symptoms (a visit to their family dr. or walk in clinic would have probably been as effective as I am sure they ended up leaving with a prescription for a puffer or antibiotic, others looked like they had cold and flu like symptoms, etc.  To make a long story short, I thought the staff were doing the best they could considering the volume of people that were there.  It really felt like a walk-in clinic at the emergency ward more than anything else on that evening.  In any event, that is my 2 cents.  I am not a dr. or medical professional by any extent so clearly I can't speak for why the other patients were there that evening but I hate going to hospitals, dr.'s etc. with the fear of catching something air born.  I go for an infection and leave with a phenomena.  ONLY GO TO THE EMERGENCY WARD IF IT IS AN EMERGENCY.  I don't know how to get that message out as it only takes one instance where that one person who should have gone to emergency does not and something bad happens.  In any event, thank you for the care and the option to get medical treatment after hours.

The reason for my surgery was a MRI confirmed confirmed 'Complete tear of supraspinatus and infraspinatus tendon with retraction of tendon to the level of the mid humeral head.' as a result of a fall a couple of years ago. The MRI was also supported by my functional symptoms. By definition I believe, this is considered a 'massive rotator cuff tear'. I was surprised when I subsequently read my surgeons operative report on the Patient Connect Health Portal. The report make no mention of the infraspinatus tendon whatsoever either in the 'clinical note' or 'operative procedure and findings' sections.  I pointed out the discrepancy in writing to my surgeon. I also reminded him that I am a very active individual (100+ golf rounds per year, scuba diving, daily gym visits). During my procedure, a synovectomy and a bicep tenotomy were performed in addition to the rotator cuff repair. I was concerned on a number of fronts. There was no mention of long head bicep tendon issues in my MRI although I can appreciate this may only be evident during the surgery. I am most concerned that 'the rotator cuff was reconstructed using a single 5.5 mm CrossFT anchor simple suture augmented with 2 dog ear loops. 1 anteriorly. 1 posteriorly anchored with 3.5 mm PopLok anchor(s).' I remain unsure if this is the appropriate procedure for my massive tear. The indication that operative reports are done on auto-pilot isn't comforting. Nor are the indications that MRIs are often incorrect. In my case, the level of tendon retraction was apparently misrepresented and was only 2 cm, later in the conversation 1.6 cm, which would make the tear somehow less massive. My request to have another MRI on a priority basis to clarify the issue was deferred due to the continuing inflammation in the shoulder which would somehow affect the imaging. My opinion is that both me and my surgeon are hoping that biological healing and repair will be sufficient or my active lifestyle.

Comment: Up to and including surgery everything was fine and went well. It was in post op that I had a bit of an issue.  I must start by saying I do not have any issues with anesthetics, I recover very well.  Having said that I do suffer from an allergy of scents and have a torn bicep in my right arm, the bp monitor had to go on my right arm as I had surgery on my left hand.  Waking up in recovery, after 10 or 15 minutes I was preparing to go to recovery.  My nurse informed me she would put my name on the list.  There must have been at least 15 patients in the post op, no doubt a very busy day with surgeries.  I was very happy to say I was ready to be on my way.  This list I never heard of, perhaps only used when it is very busy.  Looking around the room I am sure nobody else was in the condition that I was to the extent that they were ready to proceed to recovery room.  So I waited.  Then the attending nurse to a patient across from me had applied some cream that was heavily scented I insisted to the nurse to move me to recovery, she only moved me to the other side of the isle.  Mean while the bp monitor creating discomfort in my arm going off every few minute.  Seconds later the little nurse that applied the smelly cream walk past me several times, leaving a scented trail.  Destined for a migraine I urged my nurse to take me to recovery.  She simply ask the nurse to stay away from me.  Finally over an hour later, migraine intact, I went to recovery.  I found there the patients were in no hurry to leave.  I was very frustrated. There was patients in the post op and recovery before me but not in any condition to leave.  Me on the other hand ready, willing and able and not allowed to because of priority of order. As far as I am concerned that is nonsenses.  If I was ready before someone who has been in post op longer I should not have to had to wait.  Also coming out of surgery I don't think any patient wants to smell any strong scents coming out of anesthetics. Comment: I am a XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX who works in another hospital in the XXX, so I am familiar with the challenges and general expectations for a hospital stay. Ultimately, the unfortunate part of healthcare (in XXXXXXX) is that the experience boils down to the nursing staff you encounter during your visit. Nurses ultimately spend the most time with the patient and therefore play one of the biggest roles in making or breaking the experience overall. Within my visit there were huge differences in the care provided by different nursing staff, and that's unfortunate because I had some excellent staff and then I had staff that, had I not been health literate and well educated about my care and resources available, would have completely allowed major issues post partum to develop. For example- I believe that all patients should be offered a consult with the lactation consultant if they wish to breastfeed- something that one nurse agreed with and another felt I could just 'call the hotline once I am home' (not the same thing as ensuring a proper latch in person! prior to discharge! before a long weekend where Public Health nurses wouldn't be able to help!). A unit wide class daily is a good start, but for patients who have their babies in the wee hours of the morning a referral should be made prior to discharge (who can stay awake to attend a lunchtime class when you gave birth 4 hours prior). There are widespread issues in all XXXXXXX hospitals (ie. insufficient staffing) but I don't believe these should also dictate the care to patients (ie. 'go walk around for a few hours as we will have more staff available at the 7:30 pm shift start)- but this is not the fault of your hospital alone. Ultimately, some recommendations I would suggest to improve the birthing experience: ensure nursing staff (or other staff as appropriate) offer assistance with ALL firsts (first diaper change included- how many people have changed a diaper in their life?), guidance on latching OR bottle prep/feeding depending on the parental choice for feeding, ensuring proper postpartum follow up (for mom and baby- how many people know that you need a f/u 24- 48 hrs post discharge for baby?), and please, PLEASE- could you ask the nursing staff to be more generous (or at least not so hostile when asked) with supplies for mom and baby- pads, diapers, peri bottles- these aren't coming out of nursing salaries directly but many nurses act as if they are. XXXXXXXXX doesn't provide a 'must bring to hospital' list or 'not provided by XXXXXXXXX list so why would one assume that you do not have a single diaper to spare? Clearly this is all budget driven as all of healthcare is, but the patients should not feel the brunt of the managerial stress regarding budgeting and supplies.

Comment: I filled out the survey manually before I read that it could be filled out online. I was in hospital from XXXXXXXXX to XXXXXXXX, and not XXXXXXXX as you indicated. One Asian male nurse who was assigned to me pricked my arm 5 times before he called another nurse to assist. I thought the norm was after 2 punctures and not 5. Then the second nurse was an Asian female nurse and when I told her I was pricked with the needle multiple times, she told me not to complain because that was normal. She then pricked me 4 times. So in a matter of 10 minutes, I was pricked 9 times. The last nurse placed the needle interstitially, and a huge bump appeared on the inside of the elbow. The lump was the size of an orange and when I called the nurse again, she seemed annoyed and pulled the needle out. Then a third nurse came and found the vein and it appeared to be okay. I was on the stretcher for most of the day on XXXXX, all of XXXXX evening to XXXXXX and no one gave me any water. I asked several times and they just ignored me. Although I was in for bleeding ulcers, I was still thirsty and wanted water. At one point I walked with my IV to the rest room and someone dropped something on the floor. A lady who looked like she was from the maintenance department walked by and I told her there was something on the floor and someone may trip and she barked at me 'I AM NOT A NURSE'. I knew she wasn't a nurse, but her attitude was appalling. Similarly when I was told they had a bed for me on the 2nd floor, I jokingly said, 'I hope it's not a cover-19 ward. The nurse said it was. I was fearful and no one would talk to me about it. I was tested in emergency but they didn't have the results yet. I was negative, but that period of time brought me lots of anxiety and no one would explain to me why they were taking me to a covid-19 ward. Later when I was on the ward, the nurse there was very nice and brought me juice and water and explained everything. However, the discharging doctor was horrible. She asked a question. I attempted to answer it and she told me to 'hurry up'. I realize they are all busy but I was a patient, and if I need more time, then they should have provided it. I felt like telling her to go back to med school and learn about bedside manners. She agreed to discharge me after she asked me if I wanted to go home. I replied in the affirmative and she said okay. I was not impressed with her at all. I later asked a male nurse why they wrote Dr. XXXXXXX (I can't remember the exact name) on the board in my room when another doctor came by. The nurse said they may have switched duty times because it was a weekend. So, I don't know who the awful doctor was, but she probably signed the discharge papers. She looked like she could have been from one of the Arab countries. I am not certain how I can describe her but she was young. The hospital has room for lots of improvements. You should have the 'Balanced Score Card' program so you can measure all the fallacies and try to improve. Thanks ... XXXXX PS I forgot to say that a few weeks ago a lady called me and said she was from XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and asked me all kinds of questions. Later she informed me she was a volunteer. Again, I was appalled. I would have never given a volunteer all the information. I thought it was a staff person from the hospital. So if you send people to call patients, please tell them to inform the patients first as to who they are. Thanks again.

I pointed out that there was a psychiatric ward inpatient unit therefore they must have them, I was told I had to provide my own. My surgeon came in during this conversation and agreed with me that it was inappropriate for me to provide my own medications (of any kind). By this point in time I was extremely upset and in tears and I snap at a nurse. I then apologized and pointed out that this is what a patient who has not received the appropriate medications 'looks like'. I was begrudgingly given the appropriate meds. I have had several non-psychiatric admissions and have never been told that I had to provide my own medications. Comment: I gave birth via c section at XXXXXXXXXXX in both XXXX and XXXX. In XXXX I had benefits and had access to a private room. I remember asking my husband if we could stay longer while in the private room. The nurses were so fantastic. They were friendly, knowledgeable, helpful and kind. My husband commented that he felt like we were the only ones there, based on the level of care we received. During our stay this past XXXXXXXX in the shared room ... I noticed a huge difference. We did have one great nurse at the very beginning, but the rest made us feel like we were an inconvenience or and always seemed rushed. I understand that there are busier times than others, but it seemed like every question we had was an inconvenience. And it was on the mild side for us - the two other women who shared the room with us I felt were actually disrespected by some nurses. They were spoken to like they were idiots. I offered the food I brought from home to my bedmate and she gladly took some. The other woman we shared the room with was having trouble breastfeeding. I can't even begin to explain how little help the staff was giving her. It sounded like she just needed help with her latch and it seemed like the nurses were just pushing formula on her. (Her doula eventually got her daughter to latch well). I don't want to knock on the nurses completely, because I've had only amazing things to say about them based on my first experience. Comment: I had cellulitis that was severe enough to need IV antibiotics. In the past subsequent visits would be to an out patient office to get the IV but this time I had to be triaged every day! It was such a waste of time having to go in and wait to be triaged, then wait in another room to see a different doctor every day. Every day the different doctor would diagnose me again and only then would I be started on my IV antibiotics. It was very very frustrating and a complete waste of time for the doctors. The last day I was there the doctor that day wanted me to see the infectious disease doctor the next day. I came early so I would see him. I got there at 7:30 am. I waited all day to see him. I kept speaking to the nurses asking why I hadn't seen him yet as he had taken other patients before me. I could not leave the waiting room for fear of missing my name being called. It was awful! I had my treatment done by 9 am but didn't get to see the specialist until 5:30. I wanted to leave but was told that I wouldn't get any oral antibiotics unless I saw the specialist. It was absurd!! It was my 5th day of my IV and my infection was practically impossible to see but the nurses would not listen to me and kept telling me I needed to wait. I spoke to the nurses many times but I was not annoying or rude but it made no difference. Finally I saw the specialist who apologized that he had missed me earlier saying that he saw me sitting and waiting as early as 10:30 am but wasn't told that I was there for him. I was so mad I could barely speak. He looked at my area where the cellulitis was asked a couple of questions and gave me oral antibiotics to take for the next 5 days as is always prescribed in this situation. I have only had this 3 times in the last 4 years. Not a big deal. The infectious disease doctor wasn't worried either. I will try to not go to this hospital again. The complete disregard for patients waiting is unbelievable. That day I saw 3 patients waiting only to be informed that they were taken to the wrong spot to wait. They had been there 3 hours with me and then were taken to the right place to wait again. There are so many waiting rooms in this hospital that it looks like it isn't busy but that's because the patients are hidden away to wait forever. The nurses and doctors stand around talking and laughing and ignoring patients. I was lucky that I got good nurses but I witnessed patients being treated badly by nurses and orderlies. One XX year old woman and her XX year old daughter were waiting much longer than me one day. The XX year old had been there since 9 that morning with her daughter. Neither had been offered anything to drink or had been given any help. After I was done my 4 hour visit to get IV antibiotics, I went to the cafeteria and bought them each a sandwich and juice. They were starving! The issue was simple. They needed to hear from a health official to find out if the elderly lady needed a tetanus shot from a squirrel who's claw scratched her. She was still waiting when I left but I did call 311 and get in touch with someone who could connect me to the person they needed. I got in touch with them in 5 minutes yet the people behind the desk didn't bother to do this at all. It wasn't until I got in touch with them that they though oh someone is doing our job we better do it it now. Unbelievable!

Comment: I had concerns about having the coronavirus, given I had been ill with cough, etc., for a couple of weeks, improved, and then suddenly gotten worse with bad cough, shortness of breath, and had indicated that I was a mature student in an educational setting in which I had recently sat next several Iranian international students, one of whom had family visit her from Iran within the previous few weeks. I had called my family doctor who had told me to not see her but call XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, finally reached after more than an hour on hold, told me I needed to immediately proceed to my closest hospital ER room, asked which one I was going to and told me they would call ahead and let XXXXXXX's know I was on my way. When I arrived at XXXXXXX's and was talking to the nurse at the main first intake desk, she laughed and said XXXXXXX's hadn't received any information from XXXXXXXXXX in years, confirming my prior belief that XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX is a useless service staffed by incompetent call operators (if you knew that your service would not really be providing (any?/useful?) info on a potential covid 19 case coming to a hospital, why on earth would they inform the patient that they were going to doing that?). I was coughing heavily at the time and was not offered a mask for at least 10 or 15 minutes after I had been checked in and was sitting in the waiting room with other random people. Eventually a chest X-ray was ordered, which came back clear, and as I had never noticed a fever (I and many in my family do not often get fevers, even when very ill, and I informed the docs, nurses of this), and had not myself travelled out of the country, I did not qualify for the Covid 19 test. I understand the limitations on PPE and testing capacity as well as evolving understandings of the coronavirus at the time, but what really floored me was that as I was having my final conversation with the ER doctor, I specifically asked him if (given everything going on in the world - we were only a couple of days before the entire economy shut down), I and my immediate family should self-isolate for a period of time and he very clearly told me that no, there was absolutely no reason to self-isolate at all. Even now I can't really fathom that response. That doctor must have been living under a rock. And it bears repeating that this entire odyssey stemmed from a conversation between me and my husband that I might have the virus and should get proper medical advice, and started with me phoning my family doctor's office for said advice. I later read that a peripheral pink-eye symptom was observed in some patients, and I did have that one day, as did one of my children. Will there be any organized process for people such as myself to obtain a reliable antibody/serology test so that I and my immediate family can know if we may already have some covid 19 immunity?

Comment: I have always had an excellent and professional experience at XXXXXXXX especially when I had to be admitted the nurses were excellent.

I have Alzheimer's and I can only communicate in Polish. I do not feel that the Emergency staff are sensitive enough to the needs of people with Alzheimer's/Dementia. It is a challenging mental health illness where people afflicted with this condition are vulnerable and trusting therefore at risk for isolation and abuse. Perhaps a strategy needs to be developed on how to manage people who have Alzheimer's/Dementia arriving in Emergency. People with Alzheimer's/Dementia come to Emergency as there is nowhere else to turn to. We don't need to be sending people with Alzheimer's/Dementia to Emergency & consuming time & resources. However we also need to be able to perform tests, x-rays, etc. in an effective manner to identify possible health issues and provide health action plans to move them out of emergency as quickly as possible (either for more treatment or back home). It's confusing, adds high anxiety and stress for individuals with Alzheimer's/Dementia to keep them in Emergency located in the hallway with the noise and activity that exists, waiting for hours for tests to be performed, where they can't eat/drink, lack of ability to toilet in a manner they are familiar with, unfamiliar people coming/going from the space they are occupying. This is torture for someone who is not mentally well. Routines, calm environments, dedicated and consistent attention by individuals helps with the well-being and healing of an individual with Alzheimer's/Dementia.

Then she disconnected the machine for me, wrapped the cords around my neck and said 'don't strangle yourself - let me know when you want me to reconnect these' and left. The experience made me feel very unsupported and concerned about the quality of care I would receive from the rest of the staff. I wanted to leave immediately, but we had to wait until 3 am for the doctor to come in. Fortunately, after my encouragement, she did an exam and realized I was in early labour, so I was able to be discharged back into the care of my midwife and I went home. I was very relieved to not have to give birth at XXXXXXXXX. It isn't right for a patient to be treated as a nuisance for simply existing, nor is it appropriate to be told you need close monitoring only to later find out that no one is watching you at all. While some of the doctors and nurses were courteous, the overall sense that there might be something wrong but no one was paying attention caused a great deal of anxiety for no reason. We ended up having a home birth that went without incident, and felt that it was unnecessary to be kept in the hospital for 12 hours when there was really nothing wrong - perhaps if someone had been watching us, we could have gone home much earlier and had a less stressful experience, and gone into the birth better rested.

Comment: I understand and accept the nature of the dynamics of applying a fixed supply of resources (staff for example) to an unpredictable demand. I had this view in mind in answering this survey.

I understand that aspects of my survey have very low scores. Let me elaborate on why that is. The time I spent in emergency was not longer than I expected, I think the pace I was moved at was reasonable. The time it took to be processed from one area to another created no problems for me. The information I received was accurate and helpful, and I am recovering well using the guidance given to me by staff. However, the person who performed my ultrasound was very rude to me when I attempted to ask questions about what results she was seeing. She also performed a vaginal ultrasound, which I found to be invasive and unnecessary. The person who performed the procedure reacted aggressively when I tried to make inquiries. It felt as if she was trying to shut me up and it made me feel dehumanized. My next issue was the lack of communication with my family once I was admitted to my surgery. My mother and sister attempted to access information about my surgery and could find no one to help them. They are still unaware of how long I spent in recovery, surgery, etc. They were left in the dark about the status of their loved one. Instead of looking for them in the waiting room, the doctor looked for them in my room. When she did not find them there, there was seemingly no further attempt to locate them and relay information to them by the staff. They made one attempt then immediately gave up. There was no attempt made to put my family's mind at ease while their loved one was having a surgery performed, and I believe that to be incredibly negligent. My final comment will be that I felt little support from staff when I was experiencing stress and pain. There was a point where I was in so much pain that I could not move, and when this was finally brought to a nurses attention, she didn't take my distress seriously and told me to 'stop crying.' This was probably 8 hours after my surgery. I understand that crying is not the most productive way of dealing with a situation, but it is also a natural human emotive response. I was made to feel hysterical after I had an organ removed from my body. It really seemed like she was trying to serve her own desire to not hear me crying rather than help me be in less pain. It really seemed like through a lot of my stay at the hospital that no one at all cared about my well-being, which made the experience of having surgery for the first time somewhat traumatizing. I felt like I was an object on an assembly line rather than a human being. Even as I climbed onto the table in which my surgery was being performed, the doctors were quick to remind me about getting my healthcard renewed as soon as I could to avoid fees. I can't think of a less appropriate time to bring up money than when a patient is minutes away from being cut open. In the future, I will be going to a different hospital in order to seek treatment. I have been admitted to hospitals in the past and have never had an experience that has affected me this way. I am not trying to disparage the hospital for personal reasons, I am simply being honest about my experience.

Comment: I understand that hospitals and our medical systems require more funding and that nurses and PSW's either work long too hours and/or do not always make a sustainable living for the duties they perform (many I'm sure, especially minorities, feel exploited) but many of the individuals that I encountered following my surgery and during my stay at XXXXXXXXX were unfriendly, bitter, and lacked social communication skills to make me feel confidence ie: my care. I understand that each person is unique and can either be introverted or extroverted, shy, tired, frustrated, etc. during their shifts, but given the profession they have chosen, many of the staff during my stay in the hospital lacked the basic social skills required for their job. I think this could be attributed to a lack of training and/or a personal bitterness that may be attributed to their working conditions, i.e., low pay, long hours, not enough hours to sustain a living, lack of respect from their supervisors and some patients, etc. Here are some situations I encountered with unfriendly, socially inept staff: I was asked to check in with admission on the day of my surgery at 5:30 a.m. When I arrived, 15 min. early, no one was in the cubicles in the admissions dept. As other patients started to arrive, the office and cubicles were still empty. Hospital staff did not arrive for work at admissions, until 6:45 a.m. (there was one female staff who arrived at 6 a.m. to set up, but she did not address me or the other patients ... simply ignored us. Of course, I and the other people waiting were stunned. When I was much younger and began my career, I learned that if I was work for late, I would be fired. What on earth is going on with punctuality today, especially in a hospital setting? As this was my second stay at XXXXXXXXX in a year (I had my first (XXXXXXXXX and then my second knee replacement XXXXXXXX), I did, however, find a 'great' improvement from my first stay in XXXXXXXXX. This time, nurses identified themselves upon entering the room, wore name tags and completed information on the white boards in my room. And all staff wore a top that identified them clearly from anyone off the street.. But the PSW's require way more training in greeting and taking care of the patients in a friendly and caring way, thus making the patients feel comfortable, safe, and cared for. There was (I think she may have been the PSW supervisor - middle age woman from the Philippines), during my stay who made me feel very uncomfortable and vulnerable. She was a bully, impatient, rude and abrasive each and every time she entered my room. And I overheard her treating her coworkers the same way. In fact, every PSW that attended with me was unfriendly and curt. And, the cleaning of the washrooms, which are shared with other patients, still needs a lot more work. The floor became filthy as did the toilet and sink. I was worried that I could easily catch a bug or infection from the lack of sterility and cleanliness. When it was time for me to leave upon discharge there was not one wheelchair to be found. My husband had to take the elevator and search throughout the hospital to find one in order to take me to the car. Not one staff person seemed to care and help. The search took close to one hour. However, on a more positive note, the entire staff of the Fracture Clinic, physicians, reception, etc. are most friendly, upbeat, and very, very helpful. The reason I chose XXXXXXXXX for my surgery is due to the excellent reputations and credentials of the physicians and specialists. They are world class and for this XXXXXXXXX can be proud. BUT there's still a lot of work to be done in training support staff within the hospital re: social skills and appropriate communication towards not only patients but coworkers as well. Again, I well understand the stresses and strains that these individuals are under in their jobs, especially working in a large city hospital in a cias diverse as XXXXXXX. But a smile, word of encouragement, explanation of procedures, and basic respect for each other and their coworkers can go a long way in helping patients feel better and less vulnerable when recovering from surgeries.
