Comment: I was admitted for a m trail valve clip, requiring a general anesthetic and an overnight stay.  The medical and nursing care was excellent and as a retired XXXXX I am in awe of our nurses today, they are great

I was admitted for a scheduled hip replacement.  My experiences in the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, Pre-op clinic, and on the day of surgery (until I was transferred to the ward from recovery room - XXXX) were all very positive.  I was impressed with everyone along the way.    Unfortunately, I found the quality of care to be significantly inferior once I was admitted after the surgery.  I stayed only one night, and it was a terrible experience.  None of the nurses introduced themselves.  My primary concern was that my pain was not controlled from about 5pm postop until the next morning.  When I realized that I was experiencing pain when the local was wearing off, I let the RN know.  She offered me plain Tylenol.  I indicated that I was experiencing quite a bit of pain already.  She responded by telling me that I could have oral hydromorphone, but since it was ordered 'prn' I would have to make sure I asked for it.  She gave me a dose, and it took about 1 hour to have any impact, and the effect was lasted just a short time (30-60 minutes).  Feeling that the pain was coming back, I asked the new nurse for another dose.  I was told that I could not have anything as it was too soon.  I suffered for the duration and requested a dose when I was allowed.  The next dose did nothing to alleviate my pain which was much worse since it had now been uncontrolled for a longer period of time.  Again, I asked for something to control my pain and was told it was too soon.  Eventually, I asked the RN to contact the doctor because I was in so much pain.  I believe she did, however, I was only given the option of the same dose of hydromorphone (oral) or to switch to Percocet.  I have a pharmacy background, so it did not make sense to me to switch to a less potent narcotic, when I was on the hydromorphone.  I asked the RN if it would not make more sense to stay on the drug I had already started and perhaps increase the dose, etc.  I was told that was not an option.  The RN also shared with me that the doctor would not come and assess my pain.  I asked what the doctor's name was - I was not given a name, but told that it was 'Ortho on call'.  At this point, I chose to stay with the hydromorphone.  I suffered in pain and crying until almost the morning when the pain seemed to be more controlled.  In the morning, the resident consulted the pain service.  I learned in speaking to the MD that they are available 24 hours on call, and that there were many more options that could have been tried - decrease interval, give an injection, etc.  I don't understand why I was allowed to suffer and the pain service was never called.    Another concern I encountered during my admission was what seemed like a disconnect between the pre-op clinic and what I was actually ordered in hospital.  I provided a full medication history in the pre-op clinic, including providing the name and contact for my pharmacy where my prescriptions were dispensed.  When I was admitted, my regular medications were not ordered.  One medication was zopiclone 10 mg.  Instead, I was given melatonin for sleep.  I explained to the RN that I normally took a high dose of zopiclone (and had been on this for about 7 years) so the melatonin (which I also take) would not work alone.  Eventually she came back with 3.75-7.5 mg.  Again, I indicated that this was not my dose and would not work.  Eventually, I got my 10 mg of zopiclone at 2am.  The other medication that was not ordered was Cipralex 20 mg, which I take at bedtime.  When I let the nurse know that I thought I thought I should get that, her response was that it was not ordered by the doctor, and perhaps there was a reason that they did not want me to have it.  I said that I would be ok if that was the case, but thought that I would have been told in advance if a medication was being held.  She then suggested to me that if I had brought my own medications to hospital that I could take my own supply.  This obviously was an unacceptable comment - eer the drug is ordered or it is not.  People should not be encouraged to take their own medications in hospital if they are not prescribed.  All of this could have been avoided if the medication history provided in the pre-admission clinic had been consulted.   Any questions could have been resolved ahead of my surgery.  In the morning, a new nurse was on shift who delivered me my medications unlabelled in a medication cup and said 'here are your morning medications'.  I asked him to tell me what they all were, which he did.  I was unsettled to find out that I was receiving my first dose of Xarelto, an anticoagulant, without any explanation at all.  I would not even have known that I had it, except that I asked.    The last thing that I was concerned about during my stay was the number of documentation errors I encountered.  Besides the issues with my prescriptions as outlined above, I noticed some additional documentation errors.  1) The patient summary indicated that I received a consult for physio and to book appointment.  I was told in hospital that I did not need physio. 2) Melatonin on summary was written as QAM - this is a medication for sleep and is given in the evening. 3) The discharge summary indicated that my pain was controlled on oral narcotics with help of pain service.  There was no mentioned of the fact that the oral pain regimen was not effective at all in controlling my pain on the first night post-op.  4) The operative note indicated that I had surgery on my left hip.  Elsewhere in the report, it spoke about my right hip.  I will bring this to the attention of my surgeon at my next visit.  Understanding that errors do happen on occasion, my primary concern was the number of documentation errors that occurred during a one-night hospital admission for one patient.    Although I have raised these concerns, it is done in the spirit of continuous quality improvement and patient safety.  I hope that by taking the time to bring these concerns forward that the care will be better for future patients.  In particular, I would hope that the team's attention to post op pain control would be improved.  I realize that with the heightened focus on opioids that efforts are being taken to limit any overprescribing that might occur.  That being said, it is still important to address patients' pain requirements in the post op setting.  Again, the care I received along the rest of the care continuum has been wonderful at XXXXXXXXXX.  In addition, I have had family members receive excellent care.  So, I am not concluding from my one night in hospital, that what I experienced is the norm.  I know XXXXXXXXXX is a good hospital.

However, it was like day turned to night the moment I was transferred to the postpartum side of the 15th floor. I literally felt frightened for my life due to the absence of care I received on the postpartum side, overseen by Dr. XXXXXXXXXXXXX. Before I went into labour, I was being treated by the high risk clinic for chronic hypertension. Due to hypertension that was observed during and after the birth of the baby, the nurse on the delivery side told me that I had been prescribed nifedipine -- which was a blood pressure medication I had been taken throughout my pregnancy -- and that I would be given a dose that evening. However, I never received that dose of nifedipine after being transferred to the postpartum care side of the 15th floor. When I asked about it around 1 am, the nurse seemed surprised and said she would look into it, but then never did. What was even scarier was that (a) all the medicines I had been given for hypertension prior to the birth were suddenly stopped during my 2-day hospital visit despite the fact that the postpartum time is especially dangerous for hypertensive issues and (b) my blood pressure was rarely measured by the nurses -- approximately once a day. When I asked Dr. XXXXXX about it and told him I was concerned about my blood pressure and risk of stroke, he acted incredulous, telling me that they stopped my medicines as a test to see how I would respond. That would make sense if my blood pressure were being measured (i.e., if a dependent variable was being measured to evaluate the outcome of the independent variable, which was stopping all my medications). When I told him that it had been more than 12 hours since my blood pressure had been measured, he just smiled at me. My blood pressure was only taken one more time approximately 5 hours after I spoke with Dr. XXXXXX, and despite the fact that it was something like 140/90, my blood pressure was not measured again nor was I given any medicine. I knew I had to get out of there as soon as possible, and when I did, I felt like I had escaped with my life. I felt like the postpartum side of the hospital was truly willing to let me die, and I believe this is because Dr. XXXXXX was angry at me for complaining about one of the doctors in his clinic approximately 3 weeks earlier. He kept making weird remarks about it, and he obviously was not monitoring my blood pressure despite my history of postpartum preeclampsia and my current issue of chronic hypertension.  I was discharged without any discharge orders, which was especially confusing regarding what I should do about my medications. Thankfully, my family doctor is a wonderful doctor, and I was able to get in touch with him. He told me to continue the medicine I was taking before (i.e., 300 mg of labetalol, 30 mg of nifedepine XR, 162 mg of ASA, and 300 mg of iron). I am grateful that I did, because my blood pressure was high -- consistently above 140/90 -- for about 10 days after the birth. Thank God, it has now come down. I am still on the medicine, under the care of my wonderful family doctor.

She told me that she would go up to cardiology to talk about my meds. LATER, after I had been electro cardioverted, I was very sleepy, so I went to sleep at about 7 pm. It sounded like one of those things that was described by the pharmacist as a blood thinner, but I was drowsy and decided just to take it, trusting that the hospital staff would know what they are doing. BUT. Later, at about midnight I awoke from a good deep sleep. I decided to go to the nurse's station to ask exactly what med I was given. Sure enough, it was a blood thinner. At that point, I asked that the pharmacist be contacted to clarify why she had earlier raised such a concern about blood thinners, and now I was actually being given a blood thinner. I was concerned because it seemed to me that I was on TWO blood thinners. (Note: I was a participant in the experiment called BRAIN-AF, which involves taking two pills, X and Y. X is either daily dose aspirin or a placebo, and Y is either River - xxx some king of substitute for daily dose aspirin, or a placebo. Eventually, the medical doctor for the particular ward I was on came by. She clarified that my participation in the BRAIN-AF study had been SUSPENDED and that for three weeks I would be taking a DIFFERENT blood thinner, and would NOT be taking the BRAIN-AF meds. Well, I thought, thanks for finally telling me. NOW you tell me! These two points of poor communication with the patient are the only things I wish to raise here. Thanks for listening. Well, there was one more thing. Just before I was discharged, I was visited by a head cardiologist. He asked if I had any concerns, so I told him about this latter concern. You probably were informed about these things, but you forgot because of the state of your mind and brain.' I must say that this felt very very disrespectful of me, and dismissive of this information that I was providing as a patient. It is ironic that I am being asked to fill out a survey about this hospital visit of all the dozens of hospital visits I've had with my heart over the years. ThanksFurther information regarding some of the questions (note that I had a C-section, and this was my second child and second C-section):  1) Communication between nurses about care: We were fairly certain that the nurses were not always (or at least not thoroughly) checking our chart when they started their shift. Our baby was given many glucose tests due to an initial low reading, and she ended up having more than she needed as the second nurse did not know that the first nurse had already done the first two readings and she did not communicate properly with us either, which meant that our baby ended up with more foot pricks than she needed, and it was a very confusing process.  2) I have already successfully breastfed one child, with zero supply problems and no formula ever needed. I was expecting to do the same with this baby (and since have), and was on track to in the hospital after giving birth. But because of the low blood sugar reading, our nurse (XXX - who I must emphasize was otherwise VERY nice and professional, and we are grateful for her care) began immediately talking about glucose supplements and formula, which was shocking and very confusing for my partner and I, as there was no mention of first getting a lactation consultant, or trying to keep feeding her more, or pumping colostrum so we could hand-feed her (which I did temporarily in the hospital where my first daughter was born, due to a nipple injury). None of those options were discussed or offered, she just went straight to a glucose supplement, which she administered to our baby without actually discussing with us or getting our consent, which was quite upsetting for us. I understand that it was perhaps the best medical decision to make, but because we were not given other options or fully explained why this was the only choice and had to happen immediately, it felt like a violation, especially when we were already in a tired and vulnerable emotional state. I left the hospital feeling shamed for my inability to produce enough milk to feed my baby instead of feeling supported. Comment: There were two things in particular that I wanted to bring up on behalf of my parents with regards to this hospital stay. The first is the lack of translators on site to help bridge language problems. Furthermore, while it was clearly stated on file that language problems existed and that I was the main contact person to overcome the language issues, I was never called once by any of the doctors at XXXXXXXXXXXXX when important matters were being discussed. While I was on occasion able to skip work and show up at the hospital to translate, in quite a few other situations by the time I got to the hospital, the people who I could ask for information with regards to condition and treatment were nowhere to be found. Communication was extremely lacking and very disappointing, quite often I felt very much left in the dark. The second and much more severe issue was the amount of different information that we heard from the various doctors that were on my mom's case. For example during the course of her stay I heard that she had communicative hydrocephalus and also non-communicative hydrocephalus. Two conditions where the treatment options are different. Hearing different things from doctors and nurses caused a lot of confusion as to what options we had or did not have. This definitely did not help when the decisions were laid out in front of us with regards to her treatment, we weren't really sure what she had what options were really available to us. One final point that I would like to raise has to do with Dr. XXXXXXXXXXXXX in particular. While I am sure he is an excellent surgeon, his communication skills left much to be desired. When presenting our options to us, and due to the confusion from the issue mentioned earlier in this paragraph, we obviously had questions and we were hoping that by asking questions and getting clear answers we would be able to clear up the confusion from the earlier communication issues. Instead of being patient and explaining to us what the diagnosis are, what the surgical options were, their risks and long term side effects, he opted to be extremely condescending and essentially took the stance of: 'how much neurosurgery do you know?' This really shut down any kind of communication and unfortunately as a family we never really got the answers we were hoping for. During the stay at XXXXXXXXXX, the nurses were fantastic, our interaction with them was very pleasant and communication was very good. Quite honestly, the doctors at XXXXXXXXXX can learn some important lessons from the nurses with regards to patience and communication.

She did not want to tell us the gender (even though at the lovely nurse's insistence she finally did), and she seemed very poorly equipped to deal with my care immediately after the birth (perhaps a better understanding of emotional and mental well being of a patient should be part of basic training especially in such devastating circumstances). The doctor was extremely rude with my husband, who also distraught, was desperately trying to get some help for me when she rudely asked him to assist her in clearing an area for her tools...since I was in a regular postpartum room and NOT a delivery room. Was it not for the truly caring and compassionate nurses who took care of me, I would never have seen my baby girl, and they even wrapped her up for us to hold, took footprints/handprints for us to keep and let us spend some time with her as we accepted this loss. All of my 3 living children were born at XXXXXXXXXXX's hospital and our experience has always been a positive one, however this time around when it really mattered the most, it was extremely disappointing. Given the devastating circumstances surrounding my stay, I assumed the doctors would be even more sympathetic, compassionate and focused on my overall well being, however this was not the case. Especially in a time where mental health issues and emotional well being are at the forefront of discussion in both healthcare and society in general, it is surprising that more is not done when caring for women in these very emotionally charged circumstances. Therefore, I strongly hope this information finds itself in the hands of someone who has the power to change this experience for the many other women who will come after me, in the hopes that in the midst of their tragic loss they will be able to find healing and compassion at a time when they need it the most.

These things are technically true (in comparison to many other surgeries), but I was completely unprepared for the experience of being in an operating theatre. I thought my surgery would last for a max of 30 minutes; it lasted for three hours, it involved 10+ people, and having never had anaesthesia, I also had no idea how difficult it would be recovering from that. I wasn't ready for the amount of pain and nausea I'd experience immediately after. Had I known how serious this surgery would be, I would have better prepared myself mentally. Last but not least: I was kept in the recovery ward (the ward where they keep you post-surgery while your room is being prepared) for three hours WITHOUT my glasses. Coming off of the anaesthesia was difficult enough, but to do so without being able to properly see absolutely contributed to the degree of nausea I experienced for the rest of the day. My sister, a XXXXX at a different hospital, was furious when she found out how long I had been without my glasses; she told me that it's normal practice to restore someone to their usual sensory level as soon as possible after surgery. My sister also started filling out the treatment whiteboard in my room when my nursing staff failed to do so, and she also occasionally stepped in to help my roommate (once when she called for assistance going to the washroom, and the staff failed to come for 30 minutes, and the second time when my roommate's hair became tangled in her tubes, my sister helped her undo it).

We called in on XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX at 7 am into the Labour department and came into Triage at around 8.30 am. We treated very well and with a lot of respect at every step right from our entry into the hospital until active labour. However, after delivery of the baby through a C-section things started going south. We were moved to a recovery room, where we received the baby and had about an hour with the baby before he was placed into NICU due to low blood glucose levels and we were moved into a post-partum room at around 9.30 pm on the XXXXXXXXXXX. We received visits from nurses to check on my wife's vital stats and C-section recovery regularly but I believe the resident doctor checked on her only once after our child's birth. Our child continued to be in the NICU and still had low blood glucose levels (<2.6 mg/dL) which was still low and hence was not discharged and handed over to our care. The following day, XXXXXXrd was wife was able to finally get on her feet and walk to the NICU (albeit with great discomfort due to the surgery), learn to latch the baby and be involved a little more in skin-skin, be present at feeding schedules (once every 3 hours). The next day on XXXXXXXX at around 10.00 am we were told that it was decided by the medical team that we were clear to be discharged and that we would have to leave the post-partum room by 4 pm. The baby would continue to be in the nursery and we could visit the baby whenever needed but we couldn't stay in the post-partum room anymore. We thought that this was very odd since by law we were aware that usually mothers after normal vaginal birth were allowed between 1-2 days of post partum recovery, while mothers with C-section surgeries were allowed between 3-4 days of recovery. In our case, the recovery time was <2 full days inspite of my wife being a high risk case, delivering our child though a C-section. We were offered the possibility of moving to a visitor room with an uncomfortable folding bed with no medical supervision which was not an option for us since my wife can barely walk without pain, let alone sleep in an uncomfortable place. In summary, we believe that our discharge took place in a haste, which has added to anxiety and mental stress resulting from our babies current health situation and deprivation of an opportunity to stay closer to our child to monitor him closely and involve in child-parent bonding. We have left XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, and will try to come in once a day to check on our child's health progress but currently my wife has problems even sitting upright in the car without having pain which makes me wonder how she could have been deemed medically fit to be discharged since she clearly wasn't fit to travel. I just hope that other parents do not have to go through this turmoil or else our faith in the healthcare system will be totally lost. From our experience, it felt like no one truly cared about us, especially about the well-being of patients and families, and for XXXXXXXXXXXX its was more of a business transaction without the lack of basic human empathy and courtesy.

Once the pain medication was due, I buzzed the nursing station no more than once every half hour. When nurse arrived on one occasion 2 hours late for pain shot, she said 'Yes...What can I help you with', Naturally I told her of multiple communications with the nursing station. She responded with: 'Did you ask me about that personally?' I really got my back up as that was not the point: There is system and it appeared to be broken, multiple messages were apparently never relayed. Nurse was rude and unsympathetic and told me that I was not her only patient. In a state of anger that I regretted at once,  I threatened to write a letter to the Globe and Mail, to which she responded, yes please do, maybe they will send us more resources. Once I got transferred upstairs was perfect. Beautiful treatment, perfect communication.  I will always recognize and support that heroism personified in all of our front line workers. That is not in question, but I could have died from my adhesions and swelling of intestine. I understand we are in crisis, but it is also important that recovering cancer patients are treated extreme pain. All of the nursing staff but one were phenomenal, and again I cannot even conceive of the pressure and fear that they face every day. It is really awkward finding fault with your system as you clearly exhibit the best traits known to humanity. Keep well, I hope we can defeat this virus and you can return to 'normal' lives, which are still heroic by any standard.

However, it turns out that I could have been plugged into the outpatient Palliative Care Team at any point after being diagnosed with advanced cancer, but because I had agreed to be part of their research trial, I was not able to access symptom and pain management care provided by the outpatient Palliative Care Team. My family disagrees with this, and were told by the Palliative Care Team at XXXXXXXXXX that anyone can access their services anytime during their cancer journey, as they do not just deal with imminent dying, but also pain and symptom management during the illness. It may help other patients if the XXXXXXXXXXXXX knows this and can refer patients who request palliative care management as outpatients. It seems that the research doctors only focus on the treatment of the cancer, but my family suggests that perhaps they could take a more holistic approach and include the family earlier in the treatment process, and plug their patients into the palliative care outpatient services earlier, in order to help the patient cope with the other aspects of cancer, not just the drug trial.   Despite the size of the hospital, the communication seems to be pretty efficient, particularly between physicians. One suggestion that my family has, though, is to ensure that each department updates their family contact information as part of their overall assessment, and include the names and contact information for family members, particularly the POAs, as part of their routine admission procedures. I made her aware of her error and hopefully she learned from this- though it was at my expense.  I left the hospital with this oversight and returned to XXXXXXXX with a swollen hand. The next experience that could have been more properly handled by staff had to to when  I was transferred from ICU (good news) to regular hospital bed. However, as a paraplegic with a bed sore - my family who are advocates and supportive in my care relayed the importance of having a proper bed for my bedsore to all. Assured that this was possible I was transferred to a room that was not large enough for the number of people in it. I was placed beside a sink and a garbage can that was a primary station for nurses all night. I was not able to properly rest(after being quite ill in icu) and to make matters worse the bed was not a proper mattress that not suitable for a paraplegic with a pressure sore. My family was quite vocal and removed me from the hospital after one night in this room. The doctor who oversaw my care on this floor was hesitant about releasing me but  she could not guarantee a proper mattress so we had not choice but to return to XXXXXXXX . Please be aware that I was at XXXXXXXXXX a few years earlier and spent months there & where my bedsore developed into a stage 4 bedsore.  If there is one area that you need to focus on is wound care and proper air mattress for paraplegics to avoid bedsores. My family were involved when I arrived  to XXXXXXXXXX on this last visit  and vocal and ask many questions on my behalf.  I am fully cognizant & aware of medication that was issued  but much of the care I received -my family was an integral part of asking many questions so yes mostly everything was answered as I had a number of family members present who were asking & getting the information I required if it was not provided with a list of questions. I am grateful for the care in ICU given by the nurses who were  excellent in treating me with the medication required which could only be provided by ICU(except where noted) Hope this helps someone in future.

Comment: Canadian Patient Experience Survey - Item 50  I very much appreciate XXXXXXXXXX management's effort to improve patient care through such surveys. The feedback is provided with the hope that through better training of their staff in patient interactions, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX can enhance the care provided to their patients.  One of my experiences relates to a visit to the x-ray department at XXXXXXXXXX:  My husband accompanied me for the appointment.  The young woman x-ray technician met myself and my husband at the waiting area, and suggested right away that my husband needed to accompany me to the x-ray area.  She assumed, presumably based on my appearance (I am of Asian descent) that I would not be conversant in English.  My husband could not understand at first why he had to come along, suggesting he would wait for me in the waiting area.  The technician then insisted that he was needed for translation and interpretation.  Upon hearing this, my husband politely stated that I am quite capable of expressing myself on my own.  When we were in the x-ray area, the technician started quizzing me asking many personal questions such as what I did for a living, what I retired from, etc.  I know from my professional experience as a XXXXXXXXXXXX that this person's treatment of me as an outpatient was highly inappropriate.  Her intrusive questions were not relevant to my appointment and made me feel disrespected as they were asked in a condescending manner and with a skeptical tone.  She clearly did not believe I had the work experience that I claimed to have.  I resented such treatment.  Second experience relates to another visit involving a CT technician:  While waiting in the CT scan area, I noticed that the male technician had difficulty pronouncing my family name:  "XXXXXXXXX."  After several failed attempts, he became visibly frustrated and almost screamed:  "What the hell kind of name is this?"  I stood up and apologetically told him the correct pronunciation, explaining the name's Turkish origin.  The technician's next statement to me was:  "Okie dokie, come along then, Turkey, I'll have you in the machine."  I found his attitude incredibly offensive, vulgar, and insensitive.  Having been healthy most of my life, I found having to deal with such unpleasant outpatient experiences difficult and frustrating.

Comment: I had a total knee replacement. Specific feedback: 1) The team which helped to assess my readiness for knee replacement, who  coordinated appointments, tests, admin support are excellent. They have a very positive attitude and do their best to help out and find a way.  2) The pre-op team worked very well together. They communicated with me each step of the way and told me what to anticipate (including the pre-op nurse, anesthesiologist, post-op nurses), asked me what I needed, etc.  3) The preparation course was excellent and the inclusion of staff and volunteers in talking about the experience and what to expect was very useful.  4)  It was emphasized in pre-op that pain management during the first few days was very important. My experience with nurses around around pain management was variable. Some nurses were interested in asking and following the philosophy of managing the pain. However, the night shift nurse was openly not in support of pain management and I needed to ask persistently to ask about increasing the pain medication at that time. She finally agreed but reluctantly.  5)  Immediate physio was also stressed and  I was  in hospital over the week end. It was unclear when physio was going to come and each day was unclear what the plan was. It would have been more helpful if someone would have taken charge and informed me a window when physio would be available. The physio on the next day was not aware of what the physio had said/done the previous day. 6) The occupational therapist presented very poorly and unprofessionally. The experience was a waste of time and did not reflect well on his occupation nor the hospital  7) Discharge recommendations:  suggest that there be a care team post discharge  to follow up - a week to ten days after - to ask how is it going?  How is the pain management?  How are you sleeping?  Do you have care and support?  Overall, the hospital is very good but case coordination and integration needs improvement.  Thank you.

Comment: I hope to never return to this ER again. From the moment I arrived I felt that I was not welcome. The ambulance paramedics were wonderful and kind. Upon arrival, the paramedics continued to be questioned by XX personnel as to why I was brought there. I felt embarrassed for the paramedics and worried for myself and the care I was going to receive. I was alone and not able to bring a family member with me so despite my pain, I was trying really hard to pay attention to what was happening around me. Within minutes, an ER doctor came to the entrance and quickly visited with me and asked me a few questions. This doctor was harsh, abrupt and dismissive. Soon after this, I was transferred to a wheelchair and left in a waiting room for the next 4 hours where I sat alone and cried to myself. Someone eventually came to take me into the ER areas where I was told to sit in an uncomfortable chair in the corner with a few other patients who were also waiting.  Despite some empty beds, I was never transferred to an ER bed. After another hour, I waited here until a nurse came to take blood work and prepare for IV. I had to ask what the IV was for. Then I went back to the chair in the corner and waited again. When I finally spoke to the ER dr., I felt rushed and did not feel the dr was interested. The dr did not ask me a lot of questions and told to wait for imaging. The dr also did not take any notes or examine me, no ears or eyes check. The only time my blood pressure was measured was in the ambulance and when I arrived at the ER lobby. I was sent out again to sit in a chair in the corner to wait some more. A nurse then gave me some meds for pain. I had to ask the nurse what exact medication I was getting.  Someone came to escort me to imaging and told me to follow them. I was still feeling unwell and had to ask for a wheelchair. After the imaging, I waited in the hall for a while for someone to take me back to ER. I went back to the ER to sit in a chair in the corner with my IV hooked up. The dr later came back and vaguely told me the findings of the scan. He did this as I was sitting in a chair in front of the nurses desk. We were not in a room and I felt that everyone could hear us. There was no respect for my privacy. It was like we had run into each other in the hallway and were just talking. I still did not know was wrong with me. I had so many questions to ask, but again felt rushed. The dr gave me a form to follow up with a specialist and told me I could leave. After 12 hours in the ER, there were even more empty beds. Why was I never offered a bed? What is the protocol. I really believe this was because I not supposed to be brought to XX  in he first place. Soon after, a nurse removed my IV and said I could go. No one asked if I needed a wheelchair to leave. No one asked how I was getting home. No one offered to call my family for a ride. So I just got up and walked out. I had to ask directions after getting lost and eventually found the exit. I stood outside, called for a ride, and cried at my disbelief in what I had just gone through. I had never felt so humiliated and ignored in my life. This ER made me believe I could not ask questions about my care. I have been in other ER depts that were much busier than this one and yet, I was still shown compassion and kindness. I have waited longer in other ER depts and yet, I was kept informed of what was going on and offered meaningful advice and information. From the very beginning, this ER made me believe I was not welcome in their facility. This ER made me forget, for the 12 hours that I was there, that I was a valued human being. They made me believe that I did not even exist. I never want to feel this way again and I hope to never return to this ER aga

Comment: On XXXXXXXXXXXX, I went to the Emergency Department with pain along the side of my right foot, it was too painful to walk, I had to hop on the other foot. After I arrived home, I received a call from the hospital asking me to return to Emergency before 4:00 p.m. I asked what was the reason and they said that the X-RAY showed a fracture and they have to put on a cast.  I asked where the fracture was and they said on the third toe.  I went back to the hospital immediately and the cast was put on and I was shown how to walk with the crutches.  I had to return to the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX the next morning at 8:35 and they showed me the X-RAY and said that I had three small stress fractures on the top of my right foot, not my toe as I was originally told.  The cast was taken off that morning at the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, so I only had it on for one day.  I also paid $53.00 for the crutches which I only used one day.  I spoke to someone at the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and asked if it was possible for me to get a refund because I did not need the crutches anymore, she mentioned that she would discuss this with her Supervisor, I explained that I only used the crutches for one day and if I could be refunded for the Crutches, especially as I am a Senior on a very limited budget and because I don't drive, I had already spent $80.00 for the two days going to the hospital by taxis. I will go to that hospital again, should I require any other medical treatment in the future.  XXXXXXXXXXXXX

They left him in the ER for a prolonged period of time and didn't escalate the situation even though they obviously did not understand situation. In the ER, he demonstrated many symptoms of sepsis and eventually fell into septic shock and had an emergency bowel resection. In early XXXXXX, my father was diagnosed with glioblastoma, a terminal form of brain cancer. I caught one of the residents gossiping about my dad with a nurse in the deep hours of the night when he was still screaming in pain and completely delirious -- '...he has GBM anyway...' My father is at home now, where he's supposed to be enjoying the remainder of his life. His delirium, which began in the ER when my dad was left in sepsis for a prolonged period of time, hasn't cleared yet and likely won't clear and everyday we're forced to remember the trauma of that night. Poor decisions on the part of inexperienced and arrogant residents cost my dad the quality of the remainder of his life. We've lodged formal complains through the office of the patient experience and the residents have been disciplined. We're now in the steps of lodging a formal complaint with the CPSO.  My family and I also have many complaints about the nursing staff at XXXXXXXXXX, particularly those on the C4 and B4 wards. Everyday they made gross errors. For example, on two separate occasions, they gave my dad the wrong dose of anti-seizure medications. If it wasn't for the fact that I was there fully informed about my dad's condition, my dad would have likely had more seizures and would have had to suffer through increased delirium in their aftermath.   Having said all that, there are a small handful of excellent physicians and my family and I are grateful for the care they provided during our stay. But overall, I'm deeply concerned about the level of care at XXXXXXXXXX on many levels of analysis. I don't have the time to write a full detailed story here, but I will eventually find that time so that others will be informed. It's clear to me that the only reason so many negligent and incompetent people are allowed to work with such vulnerable patients is because most families aren't as clued in as mine.

Comment: The most difficult part of the stay was having multiple nurses caring for me each day.  There was never the same person treating me.  Since I had severe pain following my operation I was given an epidural for pain control.  At one point the epidural broke leaving me in severe pain.  The nurse responsible did not do a good job helping me address the pain quickly.   Her first reaction was to give me a tablet that took 30 min to take effect.   My pain level on a scale of 1-10 was '11'.    Waiting 30 min to take effect was not a good solution. Other than that the response times for call button were not good.   Many times the button had to be pushed multiple times.  Sleeping in a hospital is almost impossible.  3 people in my room and 3 different nurses.  All came at separate times which is a problem especially at final visit of night around midnight.  Each time they left the door to the room was left open so it was almost daylight in the room all the time and the noise from the hallway was constant all through the night.  My room was almost directly across from the nurses station where everyone gathered during the night and conversations were loud.  The biggest reason to be in hospital is get the proper treatment through an operation or whatever other reason brings you there but it does help your recovery if you can sleep properly and having little or no sleep doesn't help.   I want to make sure you have the correct perspective.   I have nothing but praise for the my surgeon and the work he did to treat my condition.  (ventral hernia repair)    The surgery was done very well and I'm very happy about XXXXXXXXXX medical staff in general.   Best Regards......   You may contact me for any other questions if needed.
Code: Access/Coord of Care, Doctor/Physician, Housekeeping/Room, Medication/Prescrip, Nurse/Nurse aide, Physical Comfort

Comment: The NICU staff/team was absolutely fantastic

The night I stayed in the outpatient after ICU, was the worst experience I had medically in my life:  in a room with two very sick male patients, noisy, unhygienic and torturous that I had to stay mostly in the waiting room!!

The night nurse on two nights was retired.  She came to help out.  She is completely adequate and does things not according to protocol.  Day nurse on the first day needed a helper as she could not bed.  Not once did any nurse bring my chart to record my vital signs or refer to medications that I was prescribed  Due to me being in isolation, the room was never cleaned
Code: Access/Coord of Care, Housekeeping/Room, Medication/Prescrip, Nurse/Nurse aide

Comment: The night nurses had a lackadaisical attitude.  I loved the overall positive environment on trauma unit.
The nights were mostly very difficult, because of the noise and light

The noise at night was ridiculous.  I wear a Fitbit that track sleep and while in hospital I was getting less than 2.5 hours of sleep per night - due to noise. My pain was controlled and I could have slept if the nurses had been more considerate. Nurses talking and laughing loudly at their stations as well as when they were walking the hallways right outside your door.  Supply room doors that would slam shut each time a nurse would go in or out - this could be adjusted to close more quietly The carts that nursing used for the blood pressure and temperature taking all had castors that were loose and noisy so when they rolled it down the hallway it sounded like a train - again if maintained properly this would not be an issue. It was so noisy I closed the door to the room but each time the nurses came in to check on my room mate they would not close the door when they left - despite being asked many many times. It was not till I started to swear at them - as a last resort as it is not in my nature to treat people that way - that the door would be closed. Actually had a nurse twice loudly come into our room to empty something into the toilet flush it and leave without closing the door. That shouldn't happen for a number of different reasons including infection control. Speaking of infection control - never once did I see a nurse or doctor use hand sanitizer. Nor did I smell it being used. I work in health care and know how it should be used when entering or exiting a patient environment - and it was not. Nursing kept bringing medications that I no longer took. My pre-op was done in XXXX but my surgery was not till XXX so things had changed so I understand the confusion but nursing never corrected it so each day I would have to explain it to the nurse that was trying to get me to take meds. Some would say ' just tell me that you are refusing the med and that is fine' but they would never inform the pharmacy so that it wouldn't happen again. And the meds all came in a little cup mixed together so know which pills were the ones I should and should not take was not easy since they were different brand from what I was used to taking so hard to identify. It wasn't until my last day that a nurse finally said this should not be happening this should have been fixed at the beginning of the admission. Meds also were only dispensed on their schedule. I have taken blood pressure, heart meds and PPIs for years on a certain schedule and they would not accommodate that schedule   I received daily injections of blood thinner into my upper arm. On the date of my discharge I was told that I would have to learn to self inject as I would need to do this for the next few weeks at home. A nursing educator came by to show me how to inject and explained how and where the injections should be done - in either the stomach or the upper thigh. I told her that I had been receiving the injections in the upper arm and she stated that this was not correct and against policy. Now - having said all that .... there were some really exceptional nurses ( all during the day shift interestingly ) who were very kind and courteous and professional. it was the day nurse that finally addressed the medication issue.
Code: Access/Coord of Care, Medication/Prescrip, Nurse/Nurse aide, Physical Comfort, Respect to Patient, Infection Prevention & Control

Comment: The Nursing and Catering staff were absolutely amazing. Friendly, helpful, and very good at bedside manners.  The doctors could use improving.  1)  During my prenatal care I was not informed about the preparation for or care after a C-section. I had a C-section at the last minute for which I was unprepared.  2) The doctor and pediatrician on call tried to discharge me less than 24 hours after I had given birth, while I was still feeling the after-effects of the operation and dosed with heavy painkillers. They did this without my husband being present but thankfully, I knew that I couldn't be discharged that early and asked them to re-check their information, which they did and I was correct.  3) I was taking medication prior to my hospital stay which could have side effects on the baby but the doctors did not discuss what side-effects I should watch out for. Again, thankfully I had done my research and consulted with doctors so I knew what I should do, but if I didn't this could have been very problematic 4) I wish I would have received more information on how to care for a baby. For instance, I would have appreciated it if the nurses had shown me how to change the diapers of the baby, how to give her a bath and learnt about more practical things, e.g. how much should a newborn cry and tips on how to stop the crying or showing me how to swaddle a baby. We were left completely on our own, aside from the regular medical check-ups.  5) It would have been useful to be told what positions I can sleep in with a C-section when I get back home. This was the most painful part of returning home. 6) The sofa/chair in the room were unsuitable for my partner to sleep in - they were worn out, ratty and too small. We were also not offered a blanket or pillow (or informed in advance that we should bring these with us). 7) The bed in my room was broken so the bottom right of the bed sagged down, making the bed uneven. This was very painful and uncomfortable to sleep in at night.

At the end of the day, I could easily have died or been paralyzed as a result of my injuries. I was millimeters from being killed or paralyzed  The staff at XXXXXXXXXX got the job done. Even though I was with my wife, the two of us felt as though we just didn't understand what to do. The staff seemed numb and insensitive when we asked questions such as what to next?  So we sat and waited and waited and waited in very uncomfortable chairs. Finally, we were asked to follow a nurse to another area where we waited and waited some more. This time, there were two lazy boy chairs in this area and I was lucky to get one of them. There were eight people in this tiny waiting area and we were all tired, hungry and some were becoming angry after waiting for so long. Once I got to see the doctor, I was treated with respect and empathy but that was the first and only time throughout the entire visit.. Thankfully, my problem was not serious, but could have been very serious and so apparently it was wise to go to emergency to find out but I hope that we don't ever need to go back if it's always like this.  My suggestions are to have a human being at reception to welcome and inform the patient as to what to do and what to expect. Triage needs more help to better prioritize and to actually check in on patients as they are waiting. I watched a girl next to us get progressively more in pain to a point that she started crying. Thankfully, she had a friend with her who went to get immediate help. What if she was there alone?  I'm grateful my wife was with me too because I don't hear well and so she was afraid to go to the washroom for fear that I would not hear my name called. She was right, the nurse that did finally call our name was so quiet that my wife almost missed it. .  More lazy boy chairs would be a good idea (better than artwork donated from patrons) and could actually help relieve some pain for certain patients or at least make them more comfortable. Some of the sick, injured and elderly, simply cannot sit for such long periods of time.  Thank you for asking for my opinion and I truly hope that some of my comments will make some changes and do some good.

From attachment - Given that my hospital stay for was for a stroke that further destroyed poor handwriting, I prefer typing. The following comments pertain to the patient rooms and the further to the doors and in the tests and procedure areas ie, CAT scan, MRI etc. Patient rooms: It is obvious that the repairs and renovations budget is inadequate to maintain the facility. The rooms are long overdue for the most basic wall patching and painting. The design consultants assumed chair rails would be sufficient to protect the walls, ignoring the movement of the beds and stretchers. The walls are taking a severe beating. The drywall area below the chair rails should be covered with appropriate wall protection, reducing significant future maintenance costs. Doors & hardware: The controls for the odor operators in the secure areas where patients are taken for various tests not only function abysmally, but reveal a less appropriate functional design. I strongly suspect that this deficiency dates to the commissioning of the building and the electrical designer is likely the culprit, rather than the electrical subtrade. Unfortunately the opportunity to address this during the warranty period seems to have been ignored. The specified hardware and controls appears to have been a poor choice. I would suggest that a THunder Bay firm with proven capabilities for the supply and installation of such hardware diagnose the problems with the existing installation and suggest corrective measures. Careful thought as to the functional operation of the doors has to be addressed. Hospital staff are usually moving patients in wheelchairs or on stretchers in these areas and the operators need to be located to suit.

Your night staff are often excellent, dedicated, and kind, your day staff are often acceptable also, and your Emerg. doctors are always very very good. That said, as I have a number of ongoing health issues & a history of serious cardiac issues which are proving to be challenging to myself & I suspect to your staff; I feel that endemic problems with followup & procedures are .are perpetuating my need for emergency health care. While I understand the importance of discluding my history in the process of diagnosis, each non-cardiac related visit has focused on them repeating the same upper chest x-rays & tests. This unnecessarily expensive for you, and unhealthy for me. I've been in emerg. several times in the past several months. After over 4 months I still can't hold down food, feel sick at the sight of food, have constant abdominal and back pain, an abdominal lump that's not going away, bowel issues, weakness & depression. I've had an abdominal ultra-sound,an abdominal CT & repeated upper chest xrays and ECG's each visit, but have been waiting for a call to arrange a scope for over a month which was set up twice by a doctor. I want to go to emerg. last night due to extreme worsening pain but feel it's useless as I'll leave I still have no answers following the same tests or no meaningful followup to my doctors requests at all. In past I've been prescribed ant-acids, Naproxin, Statex, Oxycontin & Tramadol, & other non-Opioid pain killers in Emerg but given no answers or diagnosis. Most of those meds are still sitting in the bottle as they attacked eat my stomach or messed up my heart giving only partial and temporary pain relief at best when I took them. I've recently been prescribed CBD by my excellent GP. & it works to some measure to control the nausea and pain, but meds aren't an answer, they're a band aid. Doctors are wizards, but if there's no cause found long term symptoms band aids won't do. I apologies for running on, but in brevity, I feel the excellent follow-up your may doctors try to set up needs to be better verified. I don't wish to be viewed as a 'frequent flyer' or a hypochondriac. I realize that emerg. is for emergencies, it's not a clinic. But if I as a patient receive no long term relief or even a definitive answer and if the same treatments are repeated in emerg without finding a causality;any temporary in house pain relief is useless once I'm sent home & guarantees my future return for the same issue, the same tests, no answers, & no confidence in XXXX. I feel that better centralized verification of follow-up is the key. I hope this is helpful. Thank you for your concerned effort.

Comment: Although nurses, doctors and hospital staff were excellent, knowledgeable and provided me with top level care, it unfortunately took me 2 trips to the hospital on the same day for my case to receive the needed medical attention. The first day/night that I arrived at the hospital, I was admitted into the ER overnight, and was told I would see a physician that night (XXXXXXXXXXX - XXXXXXXXXXXXX) However, as there was only 1 doctor on call that evening for all of emergency and critical care. I only saw a physician at shift change the following morning (XXXXXXXXXXXX) at 7:30 AM I think it is completely unacceptable to have just 1 doctor on call for such a large number of patients, and I believe it would drastically reduce waiting times if at least 2-3 staff were on call every evening. After the physician saw me on XXXXXX in the morning, all I received was antibiotics, and was than discharged to go home at 8:30 AM. I was told that during my stay, I would have an ultrasound done (which was needed to properly evaluate my case), as well source other critical tests. None of these were performed, however. As my case was not properly handled, I unfortunately was back in the ER at around 3:00 PM on XXXXXXXXXXXXX with worse conditions and the triage nurses told me I had to reenter all of my information from scratch once again - even though I had just left the hospital about 7 hours earlier. I was then told to wait in the ER behind several other patients, and if wasn't for my daughter, intervening on my behalf and explaining the emergency of my case and worsening symptoms to the triage nurses for a 2nd time, I would probably have been left waiting longer than 3 hrs. Once my daughter complained and indicated that it was the hospital poor decision to send me home prematurely (before any critical analysis were performed). I was then seen for bloodwork and readmittance all within 20-30 min. After being readmitted to the ER, I was seen by (2) nurses, a physician and (2) doctors, all within a hour With my daughter (unreadable) and vocalizing for which tests needed to be carried out to evaluate my case (I had a similar medical episode happening XXXX and so my family recalled that the nursing and physician staff did back then, and saved this medical history with these current nurses and doctors). It was only after this constant and elevated level of advocacy that I finally received the medical attention that I needed, and I fully believe that had my case received the proper attention it needed the first time that I visited the ER, I probably would not have needed to stay in hospital for the next (4) days, as I have no other medical complications and am (thankfully) in a relative state of good health. This would have freed up one much need hospital bed, which could have been used by the many patients who were stuck along corridors for several nights (including myself for XXXXXXXXXXXX overnight period) and had my case been dealt with properly from XXXXXX, it would have alleviated much stress from myself and my family. I want to reiterate that the physicians and nurses did a truly excellent job with my case, and provided me all the medical attention that I needed, once my case was properly evaluated. I truly believe that the mismanagement of my case, and the resulting negative experience of my first (2) day in the ER was directly a result of short staffing (particularly of physicians) within two critical are of the hospital. I therefore strongly recommend that XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX reevaluate if management at night staffing of physicians within the ER and critical area and units inclose staffing support in these areas so that my experience and the possible negative experiences of many other patients could be avoided all together in the future Sincerely XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX

I mean, just one thing that I did notice is that there didn't seem to be a lot of mental health support staff available to people. Once in which a woman was in early-stage of dementia or in a state of mental illness, but she was experiencing visual hallucinations such as insects on her sheets, and the staff was very condescending. All they said was 'there's nothing there' and she would become more and more anxious when they dismissed her. I went to one of the staff and said 'I know it's annoying and you and I both know the insects aren't real, but it's very real to her. A little bit of compassion goes a long way.' I shouldn't have to say that in a hospital setting. These people still have dignity under this personal struggle and they could feel humiliated in this situation. 
And the second one was a man who suffered a slight head injury and started to see visual hallucinations, called object impermanence. 
He was actually a very intelligent man I actually talked to him. He wasn't terrorized or anything, he tried to use his intellect to explain to himself and staff what was happening. 
He was at the end of the hallway and there was just standing sheets around his bed. 
I ended up going over and giving him a couple candies and said if you want to hang out, we can. He was very lucid when I talked to him. 
He was not attended to for a long time at the end of the hallway and was feeling pretty hurt and condescended against. That was hard to see. 
So one thing I think is maybe if the hospital had more mental health volunteers, peer counselors, etc. that might be better. 
People aren't gone because they're somewhere different, they're just different from themselves. 
The lack of compassion was probably from a lack of understanding, but we certainly need more mental health practitioners present. 
For the most part, other than ignoring those people, there were amusements and antics, there was one man that was pretty taxing on the staff and was following everyone. 
He decided to sit at a desk in the hallway and every time he started to nod off, 
he would bang his head on the table and the nurses would just cackle and find it amusing, rather than laying a towel down or something so 
he wouldn't injure himself when nodding off. But every nurse I had something to do with, except for one who decided to change regiments of my medication, 
this one nurse just decided you should take this medication whenever. Once I had a moment to speak with my physician, 
I asked him whether our plan for medication was the protocol to be followed, and he said yes. SO that nurse was trying to take matters into her own hands for whatever reason. 
That was the only member of staff that I didn't have a positive encounter with.

Comment: On the whole, the care at the hospital is very good as identified in the survey. Yes, there are some areas of improvement, but we were very happy with the care received. Staff are knowledgeable and friendly, take the time to address my needs, and ensure I was comfortable. I would rate the hospital very high and would definitely recommend it. My gastro, Dr XXXXXXXXXXX, literally saved my life by doing an emergency ERCP on me for my severe pancreatitis. Dr XXXXXXXXXXXXXX provided excellent care in removing the gallbladder with minimal scarring and pain. I will never forget the quality of care received by these two MDs. There were a couple of nurses who were excellent and made the stay pleasant as it could be. The areas for improvement are fairly minor and are stated here so these improvements could potentially be made. 1. The standard of care varied from staff member to staff member. Some nurses and MDs were excellent, while others were just getting by. Some of the nurses were very responsive and attentive, while others would take a long time (30 minutes or more) to respond, if at all. Certain MDs were excellent, such as Dr XXXXXXXXXXX (GAS) and Dr XXXXXXXXXXXXXX (Surgeon), while some of the other Gastros seen were so rushed, they gave the impression they didn't even want to speak with you. 2. The hospital is a very noisy and busy place where it is very difficult to get proper rest. The staff come in the middle of the night, turn on the lights / speak loudly / move equipment around and would disturb the patients in the general ward. This occurred on a regular basis during my stay, it was as though they didn't care. 3. The shift change time for the nurses was the worst time to get anything done. One nurse, XXXXXX, ignored my request for pain medication for over 2.5 hours after telling me she would be back in 15-20 minutes. The shift change process should include proper prioritizing based on the patient as oppose to a set routine they go through. 4. One major issue, in my mind, was that if you spoke with another nurse, other than the one assigned to you, they were absolutely unwilling to help in any way. Even though they are just standing around and talking with one another, they could not be bothered to help their colleague and patient with the smallest requests. For example, I required distilled water for my CPAP machine and my nurse was super busy and could not be found. We asked another nurse sitting at the desk, chatting away and she refused to obtain the water for us. I truly appreciated the quality of care received and am pleased that this high standard of care is available. From the EMTs that responded and brought me to the hospital, the Emergency department staff that triaged me, the lab staff, the diagnostic imaging staff, most of the nurses, and the MDs that performed the procedures on me. They all helped me get back on my feet and recover properly. Thank you for all that you do on a daily basis!

ff can be more empowered and given better resources to do their jobs more effectively.There is so much I'd like to share about my hospital stay. I have done a lot of thinking about it, and talking to others who have also recently been hospitalized at XXX for similar procedures. I have been perplexed as to why my experience seemed so appallingly different from others. My main conclusion is that I was hospitalized at an unfortunate time: 1) during COVID, when there was a lot of new staff, fluctuating policies, and just a whole lot of confusion all around; AND 2) during the summer over a long weekend, when a lot of services/staff regularly available were not around. My experience was of a hospital that was disorganized, understaffed, and where staff were not empowered, well trained, or well informed enough to do their jobs well. I want to mention that my answers to some of these questions require this context. Though i felt i could ask questions of staff, rarely was i provided with satisfactory answers or were my questions/concerns followed up on. So many times, things just got dropped. For example, I asked to speak to an OT; I never did speak to one. I asked why I hadn't received a spirometer and breathing exercises like my roommate (who'd had the same surgery) had; I didn't receive this until the day before I was discharged. So while I could certainly ask for things, and I did, that doesn't mean I had a good experience. In the ICU, I had serious pain which was not relieved with the first medication I was given. It was 16 hours before a new medicine was tried. In the meantime, I met with a pain management specialist who treated me with derision and skepticism. She informed me there were only two options for pain control and that she was reluctant to put me on the other option (Fentanyl). This seemed ludicrous to me then, as it does now. While in ICU, during the time when my pain was not managed, I was lucid and well aware of my surroundings, though I had difficulty keeping my eyes open. Nurses assumed I was not with it and talked about me as though I was not there. One joked about the need to get me my antidepressant medication on time. I was administered things without being told what was happening; I had to actively ask what was happening. At the end of my ICU stay, I never received a record of what happened to me there and what was administered. Fortunately, I'd had the wherewithal to ask questions throughout and recall the answers so that I could document for myself the things that happened: the pain medication that didn't work, the XXXXX XXXXXXXXXXX I received, the mineral supplement that gave me a violent reaction. On the ward, I rarely saw the same nurse during my 5 day stay, This meant that every day I was repeating myself and my issues to a new nurse. Furthermore, The staff Seemed incapable of understanding the complexity of the pain i was experiencing. They seemed perplexed that I had pain that wasn't directly associated with my surgery: muscle spasms in my back from being immobile, stomach pain from the medications. Explaining my situation over and over was exhausting and frustrating. This brought on an anxiety attack one morning during my stay. I was unable to ask the nursing staff for help, and none came around during this time, so no one knew how distraught I was. Fortunately I was able to text my husband to come assist and help me through. It was a difficult experience during my stay. I felt very alone. I am grateful that, at the very least, my husband was permitted to visit. He was so important to getting me the pain relief and comfort I needed. The resident confidently told me it was not a problem 'unless it doesn't go away'. If anyone had recognized this as X XXXXXXX it would have avoided a subsequent scary nighttime visit to the XXX ED days later during which I was diagnosed with XXXX-XX XXXXXXXX, and had a XX XXXX that showed possible XXXXXXX XXXX XXXXXXXXX. This exposes the clear risk to patients of being discharged by a non-expert resident on a weekend where staff who could have easily diagnosed this XXXXXXX such as the XXXXXXXXXXX NP (who I reached during the week by phone and was the one who told me it was probably X XXXXXXX and to come to the ED if it happened again) or a XXXXXXXXXXX fellow or staff MD would have been present to sign off on my discharge. The nurses on XX in the level 2 4-bed unit I was admitted to were outstanding. These are some of the most highly skilled nurses I've ever known, both with respect to XXXXXXXXXXX care and compassionate communication. My husband slept on the floor beside my bed throughout my admission for 3 nights which was critical for me. He was more than a 'visitor' and he provided more than 'comfort' or 'support' - he provided a lot of my nursing care (he's not a nurse). He helped me to the bathroom every time, and when I often vomited was quick to make sure I had a bucket in front of me. If he wasn't there, not only would I have been far more anxious, but there's no way the nurses could have helped me fast enough to prevent me from vomiting all over myself in bed multiple times, and the added burden on them from having to then change my gown, bed, and clean me up would have been significant. Please make it easier and more comfortable for family to stay 24/7 with patients to provide not only companionship and support, but important care. Finally, I want to raise the issue of traumatic situations impacting patients staying in multi-bed rooms together: my worst fear for the 8 months between when I had an MRI to reveal my XXX and when I had surgery during this admission to remove it was that I would suffer from a stroke. It was a very real, deep fear since I knew this possibility was with me at every moment. After my successful surgery, I was in the 4-bed monitoring unit on XX because I required vital signs assessments hourly, and I remained in that room for the duration of my admission because there were no other beds available for me to transfer to. (It was also much longer than expected because my XXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXX to confirm the XXX was fully resected was delayed by 48+ hours because they were 'very busy'). While the nurses in this unit were outstanding as I said, the impact to me of remaining for nearly 4 full days in this unit is that I could hear at all hours of the day and night the full details of what was happening with every other patient in the room since we only had thin curtains dividing us. As a result, I fully witnessed over many hours another patient in the room experiencing a XXXXXX XXXXXX and ultimately going into XXXXXXXXXXX to attempt to repair it which was not successful. I heard every detail as nurses yelled his name and tried to get him to follow commands. I watched the doctor come in to assess and tell the nurses she thought they were overreacting. I heard the nurses bring in other ceagues to see what they thought, I heard them plead with doctors on call to come and assess again, I heard them yelling the patient's name over and over again as his XXXXX worsened, and finally I heard the doctor come again hours later and whisk the patient into surgery after ignoring the nurses' calls for help for hours. Through all this as my husband and I sat together bearing witness, this patient was all alone: his wife, who spoke little English, visited for just an hour earlier in the day with another relative. To be hearing and seeing what I feared most for the past 8 months happening in real time to another person, who was alone, and to see the struggle between nurses and doctors which cost the patient precious time, was really traumatizing for me. Sometimes in health care I think we imagine that pulling a curtain gives privacy but it does not. How can we make sure patients do receive close monitoring they need while also avoiding traumatizing patients and families through this forced witnessing of such intense suffering? And further, what could have been done to support that poor man who went through that whole experience alone?

From attachment - n # 43 Is there anything else you would like to share about your emergency department visit I spent a total of 11 hours over a two day period at your emergency department in XXXXXXXXX. I visited your hospital because I had excruciating pain in the calf of my left leg. I was worried that I had a blood clot. My first visit was for a total of 4 hours. The doctor was excellent and very professional. I was asked to return the following day to have an ultrasound test done because the department closed at 5:00 PM. I arrived the following day for my ultrasound appointment at the scheduled time (noon). Then I was asked to return to the emergency department to wait for my results. The emergency room was filled to capability with people coming in and waiting to see a doctor. I was almost ready to leave but finally, seven hours later my name was called to see the doctor. If I may, I'd like to offer a couple of suggestions ... I'm certainly not a regular at an emergency department but if people must spend numerous hours waiting to see a doctor, perhaps a vending machine could be available in the emergency waiting area. Access to a simple refreshment would most definitely ease some of the stress and offer a few minutes of comfort. Also, if a patient is simply waiting for results (ex. ultrasound) from a test, perhaps the patients could remain in the department where the test was done or could return home and wait for a call. The waiting area in the emergency department was so jam-packed that at one point there was no place to sit. As well, we were instructed by the registration nurse that we not leave or head outside. As you know, Covid is a real concern and I was surprised at how many people were allowed in the waiting area. Some chairs were marked off to ensure that people did not sit beside one another but standing beside you is the same thing. Overall, I was very satisfied with the care I received. However, I was concerned at how many hours people were expected to wait to see a doctor. While waiting for my ultrasound results, there were emergency ambulances that arrived with cardiac arrest patients and pushed back the wait time for everyone sitting in the waiting area. I also observed a lady in great mental distress and in need of immediate care, which she received. It was exhausting to watch and a very stressful day. I praise the medical staff on the front lines - job well done! But, for us regular folks - I sure wish I had not needed to visit an emergency department that day. I hope my suggestions are helpful. I believe that the patients that visit your emergency department and working staff would appreciate the changes. Take good care!

Reflected in my previous answers were two areas of dissatisfaction that I wished to clarify: The first is that I did not have the opportunity to speak to my surgeon the day of the surgery. I didn't even know she was in the OR until I asked if she was there (hard to tell with the face masks.) I felt there was some loss of information between the consultation with her in her clinic, and the surgery at the hospital. I saw her to discuss a tubal ligation as a form of sterilization. During the consult, she gave me two options to pick from: tubal ligation, and salpingectomy, and after consideration and research at home, I chose the latter. During my presurgical consult meeting at the hospital, staff were not aware of the second option. I phoned the surgeon's office and informed them of my choice and asked them to transmit this information to the hospital prior to the day of surgery. The morning of my surgery, the consent form indicated 'salpingectomy-oophorectomy' which includes removal of the ovaries. I did not understand what that second word meant, and would not have caught it on the consent form, especially being nervous/hungry/tired. Thankfully, this was caught immediately by the administrator (or nurse?) I first saw that morning, and I told everyone I saw along the way, but I wish I had had the opportunity to speak with my surgeon to confirm the procedure with the person who would be doing it. I was anxious about this until I got a period after surgery. The second point of dissatisfaction was with pain management. Upon first waking up from surgery, I was in a lot of pain which I vocalized (clearly, I think, but hard to remember.) The nurse did ask me several times to rate my pain level on the pain scale, but I kept saying '1 or 2' (I don't know why) and so I was not given much of anything for pain until I came around well enough and the pain got bad enough to specifically ask for something strong. Obviously, my fault for not being clear about the 'number' of the pain, but prophylactic pain management would have improved my experience, or even being told ahead of time that I could ask for pain management. I have a third point which is a little silly, but the first person I saw that morning at the hospital (an administrator, I think) was brusque and unfriendly. She was polite, efficient, and might have saved my ovaries, and there's nothing specific I can fault her for, but I was really anxious and would have appreciated a friendly face. I don't want my above comments to cloud the fact that my surgery and recovery was easy (if extraordinarily painful) and went well, and all the medical professionals who attended to me did their jobs well and with obvious thoroughness and care, and it was an overall positive, freeing experience for me. I'd pick surgical and administrative competence over pain management and hand-holding any day. Thank you!
