Thank you for this survey, I appreciate that this hospital cares about feedback. Survey questions were not detailed in a way that would provide the most accurate representation of my visit. All questions regarding details about interactions with nurses and doctors should be separated. All staff were very pleasant and kind. Nurses asked more thorough questions about general health and medications than the doctor. I am not sure if the doctor was given or reviewed all info nurses were provided with as they repeated some of the same questions. My history is a big red flag that I am prone to somewhat unusual issues and may have further underlying unidentified issues. I do not feel that this was adequately taken into account as I later learned that my history could have actually accounted for all of my symptoms, but these possibilities were not discussed at all. At the time of my visit, I was in significant pain that was unrelated to issue I went to the ER for and did not require treatment. I have some chronic health issues that cause varying levels of pain, this can impact my ability to correctly assess and report more minor pain. The ER doctor seemed to have difficulty understanding this as a general concept and did not factor this into the assessment. When questioned about pain and discomfort related to my presenting issue, I was able to give some firm yes and no responses, but I was unable to answer others and advised the doctor that I was not sure. After responding that I wasn't sure, they made comments to confirm that I meant no. When I repeated my answer was I don't know instead of no, they moved on to the next question. While I understood everything the ER doctor said, they made multiple conflicting statements. When I asked for clarification, none was provided and conflicting information was again given. When the doctor told me their diagnosis, I explained that I have experienced that issue before and my current symptoms were inconsistent with past experiences of the same issue, but the doctor was dismissive of these concerns. The ER doctor misdiagnosed me and missed signs of a larger problem that caused my presenting issue. This misdiagnosis delayed my access to appropriate care and allowed my symptoms to worsen in the interim. Including this visit, I will have had 8 appointments regarding the same issue in less than 4 months and expect that more will be required. I understand that ER departments are meant for emergencies and my issue was not an emergency. I believe that the ER context likely was a factor in the negative outcome of my visit. I only went to the ER because I had no other choice for in person care at that point in time. My PCP is not seeing any patients in person (due to COVID) and only offers phone appointments. I am unable to go to a walk in clinic as my PCP is part of a practice under a capitation based pay model and they will deroster me if I visit a walk in clinic. I advised the ER doctor that the ER was my only option, in hopes they would try to be as thorough as possible for that setting. The visit felt as though the doctor decided on a diagnosis very quickly and framed everything else to fit that diagnosis, which conveniently is something typically self-limiting and does not require treatment. I do not fault them for assuming the simplest explanation is the correct one, as that is typically the case. However, I did not appreciate that my concerns were dismissed without explanation, very unclear information about the diagnosis was provided and they repeatedly skirted clarifying things. My diagnosis was viral in origin and at times I was told I was at the very beginning, then very end of its course and was told it should resolve within days, then that it will get worse before improving and should resolve in a month. Both scenarios cannot be true, but they were both presented as facts, not alternate scenarios that may play out. Each time the expected scenario changed, I asked for clarification abouhy as no new information was presented, but the doctor would not provide an explanation and continued to make further similarly conflicting statements. I asked about things to look for in case things did not progress as expected or things that may signal needing further assessment, but wasn't given any information. I have enough medical training (I do not mean from Dr Google) to know that some of the statements made by the doctor were inconsistent with the diagnosis they made, but my presenting problem was something I couldn't effectively assess on my own. I hoped it was a very minor issue and was relieved by the diagnosis, so at the time I did not push against the signs that the diagnosis was incorrect (not that any patient should have to do this). On reflection I realized more inconsistencies and regretted not pushing for further explanations and information. It seemed that the doctor I saw may not be very experienced or knowledgeable in that area and I would have preferred and appreciated if they consulted with someone else, passed me on to a different doctor, or advised I seek care elsewhere. I am very disappointed in the care I received, prior experiences at this ER have been outstanding and this visit was not consistent with what I would expect. Comment:
Most times ER doctors treat me with rudeness. I have a very
complicated health issues that sends me to the ER regularly. I deal
with complications from former surgeries, drug resistant biofilm
infections, intercystinal cystitis, chronic pain, and nerve damage and
collapsing pelvic floor. I am bedridden and fighting for my care I bring
my parents each time with me because most times I'm too sick to fight
for decent care and do not deserve to be talked down to or insulted by
doctors that do not understand my case or understand how difficult it is
to get accurate test results. My parents come for moral support each
time I go to ER because I usually leave in tears. I do not expect to be
cured but I do expect to be stabilized when I come in and be treated
with compassion. I suffer 24/7 from surgical mesh complications, I use
a wheel chair and there is no standard of care for those that are
permanently injured or suffering. It's would be nice to have a standard
of care for transvaginal mesh injured and not be ignored or made fun
of or slip through the cracks because there is no standard of care to
help surgically MESH injured with extreme infections and multi
autoimmune disorders and pain. I always try to bring current culture
results to make it easier on the doctors but so many times treated with
hostility. I know I cannot be cured but treating our flares and infections
and acknowledging that we suffer and live with no quality of life. I have
ptsd from dealing with rude unsympathetic doctors. I have nursing and
psw care at home to avoid having to be in hospital and be treated with
hostility while I fight for my life. I hope each time I have a flare either of
my biofilm infection or my intercystinal cystitis that this time I will
encounter a doctor that treats me and stabilizes me and listens to me
instead of trying to minimize my suffering. I have found that I have
received good care by most of the female physicians in ER but the
male physicians treat me badly. I had actually one male doctor that
refused to speak with me and put his hand up in my face to silence me.
But he would talk to my father who was in the room. I'm worried about
how patients are received in XXXXXXX ER and I now try to get to
XXXXXX ER where I am treated well always. I can say that the nurses
most of them are a joy. I have talked with patient advocacy a few times
regarding treatment of difficult, complicated cases like mine. And its
seems it doesn't really help the situation at all. I try so hard to treat all
doctors and nurses with kindness but for some reason when the words
surgical mesh complications and colonized infection issues are
mentioned I get treated with anger and a condescending attitude. I
have been on CTV news multiple times because my health situation is
rare and I am now doing a story on W5 to hopefully expose this
surgical mesh nightmare and with the hope of educating the public
about this dangerous surgical mesh implant. And hopefully bringing
about change and a standard of care for those that have severe mesh
complications. I am hoping that together we can bring about change
because surgical mesh implant complications ate becoming an
epidemic for which ER doctors are not trained to treat. Thank you for
your time.

following morning prior to the

me up to a 'ward on 8th floor'.

months sick & quarantined

diseases. When I saw 3 other
women in the room, I felt it
would be too much exposure
for 'my compromised state' to
stay & I asked to be
immediately removed from the
room. I was in the 'family
waiting room' in a wheelchair,

came up & arranged my
placement in a 'semi' in XXXX.

rib after explaining that I

reviewing them, the Dr. told me
that they did not find anything
wrong and that I could go home
and take some Aleve. I pushed
back and showed the Dr. where
my collar bone was broken and
he went back to the X-rays and
came back to confirm that the
bone was indeed broken. After
taking some additional X-rays, I
again asked the Dr. about the
searing pain in my back. I
explained that I heard and felt
pops in my back and near the
sternum when I hit the ground
and he reiterated that he did
not see anything on the X-rays.
I was sent to the fracture clinic
the next day where the Dr. put
me into a figure 8 brace for the
broken collar bone, but after a
few hours the pain in my back was too intense for me to
continue wearing it. I stayed
with the sling provided by the
emergency dept. After several
tries with the figure 8 brace and
continued pain in my back, I
called me Dr. who ordered a
new set of X-rays for the ribs
based on my description of the
pain where it even hurt when
breathing and I could not sleep.
He also prescribed some pain
meds that the emergency dept
Dr. did not, even though I had
told him that I was in severe
pain. The X-rays confirmed that
I had broken the 3rd rib and he
was able to point/touch the
exact spot that I had described
in the emergency visit. I was
truly disappointed that both the
broken clavicle and rib was
missed during the diagnosis of
my injuries at the emergency
dept. Had I not insisted in
showing the Dr. the spot on my
clavicle that was broken so he
could feel it for himself I would
have walked out of the
emergency dept with two
broken bones and an order to
take Aleve for a week. Instead I
have a broken clavicle and provided a brace by the
fracture clinic that cause
severe pain in my back due to
an undiagnosed broken rib. I
have had cycling injuries in the
past (comes with the sport) but
never have I been to an
emergency room where the Dr.
did not diagnose broken bones
and did not prescribe anything
for the severe pain I was in. I
understand that the medical
community does not want to
prescribe certain drugs
needlessly, but I clearly
indicated that I was in severe
pain in my back and near my
sternum. After acknowledging
that he missed the broken
clavicle, I would have thought
that he would have ordered a
new set of X-rays for the area
in my back that was in severe
pain instead of only the
clavicle. Not sure if a radiologist
was involved in reading the X-
rays, but I certainly was
disappointed with the ability to
diagnose a broken clavicle and
a broken rib (which is extremely
painful, even when breathing).
Not sure if anything will come of
this feedback, but if nothing else the Dr and nurse were
very polite and professional,
they just did not seem to take
my feedback about the severe
pain in my back seriously, even
after admitting that they missed
the broken clavicle. The pain
meds given by my Dr., at least
allowed me to finally get some
sleep which is in a recliner due
to the pain from the broken rib.
I have been to this emergency
dept before and had no
complaints about my care, but

latest issue. I know that the
patients need to advocate for
themselves and I did when I
was told that nothing was found
and go home and take some
Aleve, but disappointed that I
was still not taken seriously
about a possible brok

Thanks for this experience, but the multiple choice format really did not 
provide me the opportunity to elaborate in sufficient detail. Starting with
my emergency department experience I found the  to be very
poor. Having had a previous stroke and being aware of the symptoms, l
was told to attend the hospital. (XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX)immediately as this
was considered a ' 911' call. I was triaged and sat in the waiting room for
hours. At my persistence with the triage nurse, blood work was done and
I asked for further tests to confirm my symptoms. A CT scan was not
completed until I was seen in emergency.(many hours later). Doctors
assessed me at Emergency, but feedback was not given despite
requests to have some information. I asked the nurse for a further
update and she said ' didn't the doctor tell you, you're being admitted.'
My symptoms deteriorated and I went from walking into emergency on
my own to not being to walk without assistance. The lack of feedback
from the doctor intensified my stress level. My expensive prescription
glasses were lost and have never been recovered despite numerous
attempts to locate them from various departments. The Doctor's care
once on the eighth floor was excellent, despite the fact that it was a
XXXXXXX. The nursing on the eighth floor for the most part did the best
they could given what appeared to be a shortage of staff. However,
there was an incident with a pregnant staff. She was asked to assist me
going to the bathroom. She said she could not help me, given her
pregnancy and no one else was available. I declined her offer of a bed
pan and she tossed the pan on the eating area and left it there. Over an
hour passed and when another nurse requested a blood sample, I
refused because I needed to go to the bathroom. As a result of this, a
subsequent nurse took me to the washroom and reprimanded me for
refusing a test and advised never to refuse a test prior to be taken to a
bathroom. With this exception, most of the other nurses were very
courteous. I was then transferred to the Rehabilitation Facility. I was told
by one nurse after having assisted me in toileting, that he was giving me
a 'heads up' about timed toileting and this would be part of my program
as a result of the stroke. This created severe anxiety for me and a fear
of requesting to go to the washroom. It is important to note, that I have a
history of kidney problems and was on antibiotics for a bladder infection.
Because of my bladder and kidney issues, I am required to drink a lot of
water. None of this seemed to matter. After consulting with two Doctors, I
was told I could withdraw. As a result of this decision, nursing staff were
unhappy with me and continued to make we wait. I do want to point out
that some nursing staff were appropriately responsive. This treatment by
most of the nursing staff impacted my discharge plan. It was
recommended that I stay an additional week for the benefits of physio-
therapy but I made a request to leave early given the stress of the
environment. The physiotherapy and occupational therapy staff were
excellent and very tuned in to the needs of the patient. When the initial
contact was made prior to attending the hospital with personnel from the
stroke program it was made clear that there is a special program and
the would be treated as a 911 emergency. This was not what I
experienced. I realize the department is very busy but the program
should not represent a process that does not exist. Also, after discharge
I was contacted by a ' aftercare stroke nurse' who offered to help
advocate my treatment in a more timely fashion. She offered to attend
my first meeting with the occupational therapist and did not show. I left
her a message and a week later she left me a message and said she
forgot. The idea of having a specialized program for stroke victims is an
excellent concept. Sitting for over ten hours in emergency, does not in
my mind meet the definition of a specialized program, especiy with my
history of having a previous stroke. I do not want to minimize the
excellent work of some of the medical staff. I plan to write and
acknowledge these people because they deserve to be recognized. I
have a post graduate degree and appreciate the opportunity to
complete this survey. I can only imagine what it would be like for a
person who can't maneuver this process.

The only reason for less than an excellent score on some questions is that

were forced to speed up to get on to another patient, and couldn't always
spend the time with a patient, to give me time to express my concerns

are usually making the best of patient situations, calmly and efficiently,

their help. I do understand of course, that it is up to the Government to
allow the hospital to hire more Nurses, and not the facility itself. That is
why I hope that some of the comments and grades in this survey are
shared with our Provincial and Federal leaders. Also, it is up to each one
of your patients, including me, to share their feelings on this matter with
those leaders. I intend to write my MP and MPP with my concerns. Thank
you for this opportunity to share my thoughts.

Comment:
To whom it may concern, I am writing this letter
in support of the Canadian patient experiences
survey based on my son's birth and inpatient
experience on XXXXXXXXXX-XXXXXXXXXX. I feel
that it is important that I elaborate on my
experience so that it can be used to improve the
process for future patients. On
XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX I had my first child at
XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.
I was triaged at approximately 4:30 a.m. after my
water broke at home. At that time I was 2 - 3 cm
dialated. The triage staff was comforting and
informative as they gently explained how my
experience would begin as well as answered the
many questions I had at the time. I was quickly
and smoothly admitted to my room where the
care continued to meet my expectations. My
husband was working in XXXXXXX when I went
into labor and was making every attempt to get
to the hospital for the birth. The doctors and
nurses were very mindful of this, which I
respected. Nonetheless, myself and the baby
were the priority. I was told numerous times
throughout the day that since it was my first baby
and my water broke spontaneously they would need to administer pitocin. This was delayed due
to the arrival of my husband. In the meantime my
contractions were mild as I have a high tolerance
for pain. When they began to strengthen, the
nurse said that my contractions should be
comparable to mild cramps. This was surprising
tome since they felt much stronger so I
questioned at analogy. At approximately 3:00
p.m. I informed the nursing staff that I wanted an
epidural soon since I was experiencing strong
contractions. The anesthesiologist had to attend
a C section at that time, which was
understandable so approximately 30 - 45
minutes later I would receive my epidural. To my
dismay when that time came the nurse returned
to inform me that another woman who wa 7 cm
dilated and having her second child wanted an
epidural too so they were going to prioritize her
over me. I was upset of course, but it was
entirely out of my hands. The contractions
escalated in both frequency and strength
rapidly. I was in obvious discomfort and pain to
the point where I could not communicate
effectively. despite my visible distress the nurses
chose not to check my dilation. They continued
to flow in and out of my room checking the fetal
monitor, but not alarmed by my behavior. I was
never offered alternative pain management as I
awaited the delayed epidural. The nursing staff
appeared to be perplexed as they assumed I
wouldn't deliver until late that evening. They may
have based their judgements on the fact that this
was my first baby or I was not showing visible labor pains for most of the after, however, they
were wrong. It was so obvious that my
contractions were getting stronger and closer
together, yet I felt completely ignored. If they had
checked on my profess during this time the
epidural that I had requested could have been
administered sooner as I was dilating much
faster than the nursing staff assumed. When the
anesthesiologist arrived I was unable to control
my body at times just barely enough to keep still
for the epidural. Once placed the epidural
worked well for approximately ten minutes. I
began to feel slight numbing and was slightly
relieved. At this time my evening nurse arrived
and the machine was alerting us that the
epidural line was not working properly. She a few
times for 10 - 15 minutes to only find out there
was a kink somewhere. Since she couldn't get
the machine to respond she called the
anesthesiologist to come back, however, she
was busy. This particular nurse did what she
could to comfort me and find a solution. In the
meantime she shut the machine off as we waited
for the doctor. aT 7:30 p.m. the fetal monitor was
also sounding the alarm so the nurse began to
administer oxygen and checked my dilation
progress This was the first time my dilation I was
10 cm and needed to deliver immediately. As Dr.
XXXXXXX and support nus entered the room my
epidural had been turned off due to the ongoing
alarm. They were not made aware of this due to
the quick events. I was so distracted that I hadn't
realized that I was not numb. My baby boy was delivered very fast and with little discomfort.
Once delivered I was informed by Dr. XXXXXXX
that I would need a few stitches. Dr. XXXXXXX
began to stitch and I immediately began
screaming at the top of my lungs. It was
impossible to keep my body still on the bed
during this process and my sister and mother
held me down. I told Dr. XXXXXXX that I could feel
everything an her response was "no you can't,
you're numb!". My sister and mother also told
her that the epidural had been turned off. She
did not offer any other pain management options
and was entirely ignoring the significant pain I
was having at the time. It also surprised me that
none of the nurses were stepping in to assist or
say anything either. If my mother and sister
weren't in the room I'm unsure how I would have
made it through this as I was inconsolable. I have
never felt or thought I would feel so much pain in
my entire life. It was absolutely unbearable
experience that I think about daily. I felt that
someone was doing the utmost harm to me with
little disregard. In my opinion this was barbaric
and inhumane. I later found out at my followup
appointment that I had a grade 2 tear, which
would have been significant enough to ensure
pain management was in place. The stitches
were to dissolve in approximately three weeks. At
my followup appointment they were still intact at
six weeks and continued to cause discomfort
until approximately eight weeks. Overall, in my
opinion it was complete negligence not to check
my progress in a fifteen hour period. It simply takes a minute. There was a major disconnect in
communication and documentation for the
nursing staff to realize that I was not being
monitored properly. If I had been checked not
only could my epidural have been administered
in a more timely manner, but we would have had
a general timeframe on when I would deliver. If
not checking the progress of patients is protocol
then it needs to be closely reevaluated. I
wouldn't want anyone else facing the pain and
discomfort I felt this day. I refused pain
management and that's what I expected to
receive. I am hopeful that this feedback assists
with necessary changes within the department. I
wouldn't want any other person to endure the
pain and face the experience I had during my
son's birth. Regards, XXXXXXXXXXXXX

Comment:
I have always received excellent care
in emergency dept and from all staff
when admitted for care Wait times can
be excessive sometimes with people
not attending a doctors office or clinic.

I have an autoimmune condition, which was listed. I should have been told
what was in that bag, that was attached to me intravenously, prior to surgery,
whilst sitting and waiting in pre-op room. It upset my system for more than a
month afterwards. It was just a simple 30-minute procedure. I only had to fast
from 8 am onward, and was allowed to drink water up until noon. I was not
dehydrated. That might not have been necessary to give to someone with
such extensive food/chemical intolerances. That was poor judgment on the
part of the hospital staff. It was risky, and I paid for it. I would have said no
thanks, had XXXXX told me why it was being administered, and that it was
actually unknown what was exactly in that bag - which she did not tell me until
just before I went into surgery (a little too late)!!! XXXXXXXX, in recovery, was
hasty, impersonal, robotic, and too busy chatting with her two coworkers in the
room, about totally non-work-related topics, to spend much time with me upon awakening - other than to check for vitals. I was a bit talkative coming out of
the sedative. One of the other nurses shushed me for talking too loud. It was
rude. Then I heard her use the word 'she' in relation to me, as though I must
be stupid, or deaf, or not even in the room!!! And they all chuckled at my
expense. I had no idea that I was talking loud at all. My hearing was slightly
impaired from all the buzzing in my ears from the operating room. It was
humiliating, and upsetting. I didn't need to get brought down at such a
vulnerable time. XXXXXXXX had no other patients. She could have just obliged
me until I was transferred. Then I was taken back to the day-care section,
where XXXXXX attended to my needs. She was nice, but she sent me home
with minimal instructions and dressings that were too small. Good thing that
my GP's office had the same dressings in a bigger size. She also did not
inform me that if I fill the prescription at the hospital, it might not be covered on
my drug plan. So my brother-in-law filled it at the hospital and paid for it,
unbeknownst to me. He was just being kind. I would not have taken it had I
known it was not covered. I could not take those expensive pills anyway. They
made me sick, after just half day of administration. So that money was totally
wasted. I phoned the day-care department quite a few times, over the
weekend, once I was home, since I was not advised on much prior to surgery,
nor afterwards, as to what to expect in the coming days at home alone.
Sometimes those who answered the phone were kind; but other times I was
treated as though I was bothering them, or they were too busy to answer my
silly questions. It took me some time to get back to completing this
questionnaire because I am only just starting to feel better again, after
receiving whatever was in that bag that upset my system (it caused an
immune response). I also wanted to collect my thoughts, and decide how
much I wanted to share. I decided that I did not want to withhold any of the
truths about this experience. It certainly seems that medical personnel are
much nicer, and much more attentive, before they cut you open than
afterwards. I still have pain and numbness in the right shoulder area. I was not
informed about this possible outcome at all. I have no idea how long this will
last, but it has been like this for more than 2 months now. I also had a bath,
and went to the gym, ten days post-surgery, since no one told me that I couldn't. Meanwhile I was actually meant to have a 4-week restriction on both
activities. I hope that this feedback serves you well for future procedures.
Thank you.

acting insulin doses. If I did not

dose schedule, my stay could

unacceptable. If I had not been
conscious enough to explain this

died from low blood sugar and
being given insulin without carbs.

about the food being delivered
